SMPTE Journal 2025 State of Archiving article

Author: James Snyder

Date: 9/15/2025

2025 saw both continuing progress in media preservation and continuing challenges.  Media preservation currently consists of two key, substantively different areas.  The first is adapting current production tools and practices to make the long-term preservation of new materials easier once the final production is completed.  The second is the efforts to identify existing content libraries to create the best conditions for their survival and reuse, which includes planning for non-digital content masters (especially existing physical media) to be converted to digital assets to allow for future reuse and remonetization.

1) Planning New Productions to Optimize Their Survival

In the sphere of new productions, one key missing aspect of new productions is the planning for the preservation of the masters of the finished productions and their source materials to enable future reuse/resale.  Given the level of detail that goes into new productions, adding the final step after the completion of a production so that the time and money spent does not go to waste because the masters have been damaged or lost is not only a logical step but a small extra effort and budget.  In surveying production students from multiple universities and internship programs, very few are being taught to think beyond the end of a given production to how those production materials will survive after the program’s first transmission.  A key lesson in content archiving is its much easier to collect the data and plan for its storage for the long term as part of the original production plan than after the production is done.

An important aspect of long-term preservation is planning for the storage of the deliverables upon completion of a production.  Once a production is completed the usual concern is what delivery channel(s) the finished masters must be delivered to.  This is the point to think of future reuse as just another output from your production process: what format do they need to be in, and where do they need to be sent once production is complete.

For many organizations, even large studios, the answers are not always obvious.  But ask the question anyway.  Production planners already have to ask what CDNs or servers finished production files must be delivered to.  Ask one more question: where do the edit masters and raw source files and any derivatives also need to be delivered?

Additionally, a key enabling factor for long-term content preservation, the file type, has finally started to enter the planning factors for those involved in planning future productions and content preservation.  Major content producers have begun to implement the compatible file formats such as IMFs that were designed to promote interoperability between different types of equipment and different setups at various vendors throughout the various stages of production.  Likewise, those organizations that both produce new content and hold older content are beginning to wake up to the need for compatible file formats between today’s archive files, archive files created from digitizing physical media, and files involved in the production and post-production processes.  The files used in production processes today are not ideal for long-term preservation.

Production vs Archive file types

One can always use a production file as an archive file, but there are several problems with doing so if the goal is to have the content survive for more than a decade.  The first is that most production files use lossy codecs, which can cause concatenation artifacts when converted to future production file types.  The second is that lossy codecs are superseded over time, meaning they MUST be converted for future reuse when those codecs are no longer in common use.  The solution is to create an ‘evergreen’ format, which can be easily transcoded to current and future lossy production codecs, but don’t change the original content essence itself.  Such an archive file would be mathematically losslessly coded, and ideally be one of the open standards such as JPEG2000 reversible 5/3 or FFv1 lossless.  Similarly, the wrapper should be MXF or similar, since interoperability with future systems is exactly what the SMPTE MXF standard was created to accomplish.

2) Digitizing Content Libraries for Long-term Preservation

With all the new distribution channels, especially the FAST channels, available today, the existing content libraries that exist around the globe are getting a chance to be available to audiences again.  These include not only the content libraries of production companies large and small, but the content libraries that exist in major universities (such as the UCLA Film & Television Archive, the Indiana University archive, and the Library of American Broadcasting at the University of Maryland-College Park), media archives not affiliated with production companies (such as the Sherman Grindberg Film Library, containing the Paramount and Pathè newsreels), and cultural archives such as the US Library of Congress, the US National Archives & Records Administration (holding the Universal and “March of Time” newsreel archive in addition to those produced by the US Federal government), the British Film Institute, and Library and Archives Canada.

Just at the moment many of the archives around the globe are waking up to the fact that they have content that folks may want to access and make searchable (and perhaps pay for as well), the audiovisual content preservation field is facing a shortage of equipment and a proliferation of incompatible file formats.

The equipment shortage developed out of the fact production of the various video and audio tape format machines ended more than 10 years ago.  While a few experimenters have produced a limited number of new audio players, there have been no new videotape players manufactured since that last DVCPRO machines were built in 2020.  For Betacam family machines, no new players have been built since around 2014.  For VHS, no new machines have been built since 2016.  In speaking with the holders of collections around the world, the author has estimated there are at least 100 million tapes of all formats and all standards around the world.  With only used machines available to play them back so they can be digitized.

The result is a shortage of playback machines.  This involved in digitizing collections are acquiring as many machines from previous owners and collectors as possible.  Many times those holders are TV stations and production companies.  Sometimes they are older engineers and technical staff who couldn’t abide seeing the old machines thrown away and have squirreled them away in garages and storage locations around the world.  Some are the younger generation have only known digital playback and who have become fascinated with analog equipment and are collecting it for their own hobby interests.  One sobering fact has emerged in the past few years: there are more tapes around the world than there are machines to play the content on those tapes.

At this point many who plan digitization projects throw up their hands.  For those of us who know what long-term preservation actually means, we’ve realized what the answer is: build more machines.  If the original manufacturers won’t do it (and having talked to all of them, none of them will as of the writing of this article) that means building machines from scratch that can play back at least the most common formats around the world: the Betacam family, the VHS family, the DV family, and so on.  How such a design would be accomplished, and how much it will cost to create working prototype(s), is one of the current areas of study.  How to fund it is also being explored.

Film scanning for preservation

The one area of physical media preservation that does not suffer from a lack of equipment is the film scanning industry.  There are still multiple manufacturers around the world, that offer price points from $16000 to six figures.  A key challenge for those with film holdings is the cost.  While many film collections exist at the major film studios and cultural archives around the globe, only the most well funded can afford to either purchase a film scanner outright, or pay third party vendors to scan the film for them.  File formats are relatively stable and compatible, with DPX and TIFF the most commonly used for archive quality film scans.  These file types are uncompressed and can be used by the widest variety of software packages.  They can be imported into production files types such as IMF.

Long-term preservation

Long term preservation can be defined by the period of time content can or should be preserved.  The oldest film in existence is from the 1880s, and most would agree we should not throw away or destroy content that old for both historical and educational reasons.  A good starting point for how long a work should be preserved is the Copyright registration period.  The Berne Convention is the starting point, but countries like the US have extended the period provided by the Berne Convention further.  Very simply, those periods are end at least 50 years after the death of the final author of a film, or 120 years for those done as work for hire.  These are generalizations of the numbers from around the world, so if Copyright is your concern be sure to consult the appropriate Copyright authorities in each country in which your work will be registered.

But for the purposes of preservation let’s take the minimum number of years a work can reasonably be expected to be preserved as 120 years.  That means that a work created today, probably as files, will need to survive until at least 2145.  In the media preservation organizations this author has worked with the term used for designing and implementing a data storage plan for a minimum of 120 years is referred to as “temporal engineering”.  It not only includes key design aspect such as what storage systems can accommodate the data today, but how often the data will need to be copied to prevent data being lost simply from being stored on obsolete data storage systems.  Regardless of whether you build your own storage systems, or by them from others.  “Cloud” is, after all, just hiring someone else to do the equipment and software part you don’t want or can’t afford to do yourself.

Long-term preservation planning also means thinking through what types of metadata are required today, will be required for future personnel to know what a set of files are and who they belong to, and will be required to communicate key data such as copyright, rights clearances, contracts germane to the production, and any credits for the people involved in productions.  The production industry has begun this journey to understand how to generate, collect, transmit through the production and distribution process, and store in data storage system.  Efforts such as the MovieLabs Ontology project, and PBCore have started to define the extent of the areas that need to be defined.  At least 7 distinct types of metadata have been identified: Technical,

Cataloging, Copyright, Performance rights, Provenance, Descriptive, and Spoken and written language metadata.

Preservation vs Restoration

A key distinction had developed for those involved in media preservation: what is preservation vs what is restoration.  The SMPTE Archival Award Committee has prepared definitions of the two words: Preservation is where the original work is preserved in a new form (digital vs analog, file vs tape) but with no changes to the visual, aural, or data content from the form as it was recorded.  Restoration is where preserved data is changed or enhanced in some ways for reuse.  At times the preservation field crosses into the restoration field, such as where film must be color corrected after digitization so that it looks as it did when the film was originally released to the public. Understanding whether one is working on preservation or restoration makes it easier to understand what technical, and by extension funding, curatorial, and management decisions, are required to allow for content to survive for long periods of time.

Conclusion

2025 has seen a lot of progress in creating and bringing the pieces together to enable long-term preservation of audiovisual content.  That said, many holes still exist in production, distribution, and even pre-production planning that force organizations to spend money in future years to recreate plans and metadata that can and should be created and stored as a part of the production, distribution, and long-term storage functions.

## A Multispectral Scanning and Post-Processing Workflow for Historical Film Colors

Dr. Barbara Flueckiger

Scan2Screen Dr. Giorgio Trumpy Scan2Screen / NTNU

## Written for presentation at the

## SMPTE 2025 Media and Technology Summit

Abstract . The vast range of historical film color processes necessitates advanced workflows for scanning and post-processing to obtain digital representations that faithfully render the multitude of dyes and pigments present in archival materials. Our previous research indicates that optical configurations in traditional scanners limited to three or four spectral bands often fail to record important color information. To comply with core principles of future-proof digitization workflows, scanner properties and post-processing should be transparent, measurable, and science-based.

A multispectral digitization workflow that uses a uniform distribution of spectral bands across the visible spectrum can significantly improve results and provides reliable documentation of heterogeneous archival color film stocks. It also enhances versatility for innovative renderings compatible with future projection technologies and visualization pipelines.

Reducing subjective interventions in film digitization remains a cornerstone of restoration ethics. Multispectral scanning directly leverages the information embedded in historical film stocks, enabling a robust, material-based technology that respects the unique properties of each film element.

An integrated multispectral digitization and post-processing chain supports physically accurate rendering of scans by including measurements from various types of cinema projection illuminants. The ultimate goal of this workflow is to represent the color appearance as it would have been perceived on the cinema screen.

When multiple film elements must be integrated into a digitization and restoration project-such as negatives and several positives, later prints on differing color film stocks, or black-and-white separations-a comprehensive, scientific methodology is essential for achieving a consistent aesthetic representation of diverse source materials with style transfer.

Building on more than a decade of research into the technology and aesthetics of historical film colors and scanning, we have integrated this knowledge into a practical solution.

## Introduction

Over the last two decades, developments in film scanners have been largely incremental, even as the business model and areas of application have changed fundamentally.

Most professional film scanners in use today were conceived for chromogenic negative stocks intended for the Digital Intermediate Workflow of the early 2000s. When film production shifted fully to digital, scanner manufacturers repurposed their systems for archival use, making only minor modifications to their mechanical and optical designs. As digital technologies advanced and cinema projection also transitioned to digital, the dissemination of archival films became fully digital as well. This created a prolific field: Millions of hours of archival film required digitization, supported by both national initiatives and private funding schemes.

Yet despite the demand, awareness of the specific requirements of historical color film stocks by which we mean all the film color processes invented and in use before the mid-1990s -has remained limited.

The vast majority of the hundreds of color processes developed throughout film history differ fundamentally from chromogenic negatives. Their dyes and pigments exhibit idiosyncratic spectral characteristics that current scanners cannot comprehensively capture. Some of these colors are located outside of current standard color spaces (DCI-P3, Rec. 709, Rec. 2020). As a result, scans often fail to provide a complete and uncompromised representation suitable as a starting point for post-processing.

A new approach is therefore essential-one that spans the full spectral range of historical films and pays special attention to the illumination of these films. In film projection, the material composition of a film and the optical light path of the projector, combined with a specific illuminant, together define a film's unique appearance on the cinema screen.

Multispectral scanning addresses this challenge by recording the spectral characteristics of historical color films using a condensed illumination beam and providing the foundation for rendering the resulting scans with different projection illuminants used throughout film history. The ultimate aim of digitization is to recreate, as closely as possible, the appearance of the film as experienced in theatrical projection.

Equally important, every digitization must adhere to the core principles of restoration ethics: documentation, transparency, and reversibility. 1 Subjective interventions should be minimized. A rigorously science-backed workflow-combining multispectral scanning with coherent and well documented post-processing-is essential to meet these ethical requirements. It also provides the only path to producing future-proof digital elements capable of adapting to emerging standards in color management and new display technologies.

## Configuration of Multispectral Scanning Hardware and Systems Control

## Basic Requirements

What are ideal properties of scanner hardware developed specifically for historical color film stocks?

In a previous study, 2 we established a catalogue of desiderata for scanning devices optimized for archival films, with particular emphasis on accurate color representation.

- Mechanical layout: The transport system should prevent physical damage by operating with low tension and precise optical control. A sprocketless, pinless film path is required to ensure gentle handling while enabling frame-by-frame capture with a series of spectral bands.

- Illumination: The system must include an array of spectral bands spanning the entire visible range, with an additional infrared channel for detecting scratches and dust in silverless color film stocks. To replicate cinema projection, the optical path should provide collimated illumination and a uniform light path.
- Spatial resolution and image geometry: Resolution should be high enough to capture local details, i.e. ≥ 2K for 16 mm and ≥ 4K for 35 mm film. Full edge-to-edge scanning is mandatory to include precious color information and analog metadata present in the perforation area. Once the film is digitized without this information it is nearly impossible to later identify film stocks or trace the genealogy of a film element.
- File output: The camera should generate unprocessed, radiometrically linear monochrome image data at high bit-depth (>12-bit), with each spectral band recorded separately, in an uncompressed, well-documented, and sustainable file format.
- Modularity: All components should follow a modular design to allow integration of new cameras, illumination systems, and optics, enabling adaptation to both the diversity of film stocks and emerging standards and technologies.
- The user interface and controls need to guide experienced scanner operators through a rigorously defined process and restrict options to scientifically validated parameters, thus excluding subjective interventions.

Traditional film scanners only partly meet these requirements. Critically, the accurate capture of historical film colors remains the most neglected aspect of the process.

## The Quest for Color Authenticity

Film is an inherently ephemeral medium.

Film elements undergo continuous transformation during their lifespan-degradation, decay, fading, shrinking, damages such as scratches, dirt, microorganisms. Each element also carries its own genealogy, often poorly documented and requiring assessment and research by a trained film historian, archivist or curator. Negatives, positives, and intermediate elements can co-exist in multiple versions. Distribution positives printed from original camera negatives or intermediates contain the intended color characteristics, provided they are unfaded and printed on the designated stock at the time of their production. Original camera color negatives, on the other hand, provide the highest spatial resolution and dynamic range, but lack crucial information for reproducing a film's authentic aesthetics. This discrepancy arises because a) printing stocks differ amongst one another in their spectral sensitivity, their sensitometric characteristic, their dynamic range, and their dye spectra from negatives, and b) postprocessing steps such as color grading and chemical development determine the color aesthetics of a positive print, which is different from any intermediate element.

The situation is even more complex when we consider the hundreds of mimetic historical color processes-i.e. color processes defined by a photochemical chain dedicated to match visual perception of a scene as much as possible, often referred to as natural colors . Some of them are using black-and-white separations as a source material to which color is applied only in the production of exhibition prints in the lab, for instance Technicolor's dye-transfer process. Earlier applied colors were added to each individual black-and-white print manually through tinting, toning, hand or stencil coloring, producing prints with widely varying palettes.

The color-forming dyes and pigments embedded in the emulsion layers of positives do not always pair precisely with the complex color physical properties of the associated negative original. They produce side absorptions that hinder ideal colorimetric reproduction. Inter image effects between layers in the film stocks further contribute to their non-linear response, albeit to

a lesser degree. 3 Because of this non-linear and often arbitrary relationship-especially in nonchromogenic two- and three-color processes and in chromogenic film prior to the 1950s-each color film stock exhibits its own idiosyncrasies, which we describe as its material aesthetics . Even two exhibition prints produced using the same method can appear markedly different, as numerous factors in the post-processing chain influence the final result.

An advanced, historically conscious scanning workflow must therefore prioritize the capture of the color information in exhibition prints. Yet most commercial scanners were designed for chromogenic negative film stocks with lower optical densities up to 2 and some cannot adequately record the higher densities of exhibition positives, which can exceed 4. 4

While the first step in an advanced and restoration-ethical scanning workflow must be informed by the material and technical properties of the historical film stocks to be scanned, the second step must focus on the illumination. It needs to consider all the spectral power distribution of the illuminants in the scanner and of the light sources in analog cinema projectors and their optical paths.

Aiming at translating the analog colors of historical films into the digital domain therefore needs to take into account all these key factors pertaining to the source elements and their presentation on the theater screen.

## Illumination is a Key Factor

What appears on the cinema screen is colored light, defined by the interaction of projector illumination and the spectral absorption of dyes and pigments in the film. Illumination is thus a decisive factor in digitization.

Figure 1: Comparison of three major professional film scanners: The scanners produce different results without documentation of their optical properties and proprietary image processing. The outcome is also highly dependent on the scanner operator's expertise and decisions. Scans of a Technicolor No. IV dye transfer print of the trailer of SAMSON AND DELILAH (1949).


As mentioned above, most traditional film scanners employ only three or four narrow spectral bands, leaving gaps of sensitivity. As a result, they fail to capture the variability of spectral responses in historical stocks. Because these bands are hardwired into the mechanical layout of the scanners, they also restrict the versatility for a science-backed capturing device.

Furthermore, scanner illuminants are rarely documented, and proprietary image processing embedded in hardware and / or software introduces black-box operations that make it impossible to document the color management chain, thereby violating the principles of restoration ethics.

An advanced multispectral scanner covers the whole visible spectrum ideally with evenly spaced or adjustable spectral bands that are documented as part of the metadata file. It supports both collimated and diffuse illumination; the optical path of illumination is crucial for certain film stocks. Collimated light replicates the optical path in projection light, while diffuse light reduces the visibility of mechanical damage on the film element (e.g., scratches and dirt) and is therefore preferred in traditional scanners. As we reported in an earlier paper, the optical path not only influences local and global contrast for certain film stocks, but it also affects the hue of the film, due to the so-called chromatic Callier effect that is wavelength dependent. 5 The effect is prominent for film containing scattering elements, such as metal pigments in toned film.

Figure 2: Comparison of a stencil-colored and toned film in diffuse (left) and collimated illumination (right) show the Callier effect.


Multispectral scan of a stencil-colored and toned print of LE PIED DE MOUTON (1907), Library of Congress, rendered with the spectral emission of a Kinoton FP30 xenon illuminant.

In the various stages of scanner development, we tested different illumination set-ups.

Our first experimental design (ERC Proof-of-Concept VeCoScan, Grant Agreement number 812583) applied a linear variable bandpass filter (Schott Veril S200) covering the spectral range from 400 to 700 nm. This filter selected spectral bands of approximately 18 nm FWHM from the emission of a Light Emitting Plasma bulb (HPLS345 High-Power Plasma Light Source and 5 mm Liquid Light Guide). By shifting the filter through a narrow slit in front of this broadspectrum plasma source, we illuminated the film material with 25 spectral bands, producing a corresponding series of 25 monochrome high-resolution images. Each image represented one spectral band under either diffuse or collimated light. Combining these methods-using a

directed illumination path alternately scattered close to the film through a translucent, spectrally neutral diffusion filter-yielded 50 monochrome images per frame. While this setup offered the best coverage of any spectral properties with variable adjustment of the lights, it proved impractical for real-world applications. The design's additional moving parts increased vulnerability to physical damage and slowed operation, while the resulting data volume was excessive and partly redundant, especially considering films' frame rate of 16 to 24 fps.

To address these limitations, we introduced a selection of LEDs into the optical design, reducing the number of spectral bands and enabling rapid, pulsed illumination without moving parts. However, they also present physical constraints. Not only are their emission properties limited by chemical characteristics of the available light emitting materials (indium gallium nitride and aluminum gallium indium phosphide), but they also tend to change their spectrum depending on the working temperature. Careful selection is therefore mandatory. Furthermore, commercially available LEDs that meet the specifications outlined above leave a gap in the green-yellow region between 530 and 590 nm which must be filled using interference filters. In practice, 6 to 10 evenly spaced narrow spectral bands sufficiently map the visible spectrum between 400 to 680 nm and produce accurate colors. The LEDs flash into a mixing rod for even distribution, after which the light is condensed and directed via a mirror system to produce collimated illumination. As in the previous design, a translucent white filter for diffused illumination is inserted alternately close to the film.

Each illumination unit's spectral bands are measured using a Qalif Spectro spectroradiometer, that captures a range from 380 nm to 780 nm with a color accuracy of ± 0.0015 for CIE 1931 xy and luminance accuracy of ± 1%. The data points from these measurements are exported, converted into text files, and incorporated into the workflow software for metadata documentation and visual rendering. This approach guarantees transparency, sustainability, and reversibility in multispectral image processing.

## Calibration

In the calibration process preceding each scanning session, the integration time of each spectral band is determined through a series of flashes with increasing intensity to normalize the spectral response. This procedure enables full use of the sensor's dynamic range, increasing the signal-to-noise ratio while preventing overexposure in bright image areas or pinholes, which should be avoided according to DIN SPEC 15587. 4 Integration time values are stored with the project data and documented in the metadata file.

The flat-fielding process involves capturing white and black frames without film to calculate transmittance values and compensate for uneven illumination in the image-forming area.

## Rendering

Whereas traditional digitization workflows require extensive and time-consuming color grading after scanning, multispectral scanning enables the calculation of color values corresponding to the spectral transmission of the scanned film through a dedicated rendering pipeline.

Color grading in conventional digitization workflows presents several problems. It is costly, requiring several experts and expensive color grading suites, and more critically, it introduces subjective judgments. Such subjectivity undermines a cornerstone of restoration ethics: transparency. Transparency requires the intersubjective communication of decisions and interventions applied during the digitization / restoration process. More often than not, grading decisions are based on visual inspection of the scanned film or a reference print on a viewing bench in front of an LED light panel. A scientifically rigorous workflow eliminates the need for color grading completely by calculating the color values directly from multispectral scans, as elaborated in this section.

The final results of the rendering still allow for curatorial adjustments after the scientific workflow is complete. Transparency requires that these additional steps are grounded in expert knowledge and fully documented. Enhancements such as increasing saturation, sharpening, and other alterations must be identified as re-mastering. Customers may request adjustments to suit contemporary viewing preferences or adjust content for distribution platforms that differ from cinema projection, which is a common practice guided by economical demands. These additional processing steps can be accommodated, provided the unaltered multispectral raw scans and scientifically derived renderings are safeguarded in the processing package, accompanied by expert documentation to the metadata for each version.

Once the film has been scanned multispectrally-frame by frame, with a series of narrow-band illuminations in diffuse and / or collimated light as mentioned above-the resulting stacks of monochrome representations need to be processed to produce a color rendition that matches the source film as projected on the cinema screen. Color values are computed from the transmittance images using colorimetric calculations that take into account an illuminant and the color-matching functions for a 2° CIE 1931 standard observer. Renderings are output in established image file formats such as DPX or TIFF as tristimuli (DCI-XYZ) or RGB values (DCIP3, Rec. 709, and Rec. 2020) and can be ingested into any major video post-processing and color grading software.

The visual rendering software incorporates measurements of the spectral power distribution of typical illuminants used in cinema projectors throughout the course of film history. These measurements were carried out with a Qalif Spectro spectroradiometer that recorded the light reflection from a Spectralon tile using a collection of historical projection lights. The set includes carbon arc (high intensity arc and low-intensity arc), 6 limelight, halogen light, incandescent light, xenon, pulsed super-high-pressure mercury lamp, metal halide sources, later extended to include additional lights-halogen illumination, LED light panel. For instance, we measured carbon arc illuminations at Kinemathek / Lichtspiel in Bern, Switzerland, using a historical Westrex Master 35mm projector (Century Projector Co., Ashcraft Manufacturing Co., NY) from their collection, recording both low intensity and high intensity arcs. 7

Figure 4: Measurement of the spectral power distribution of a high-intensity carbon arc projection illuminant.


Executed with a Qalif Spectro spectroradiometer and averaged over 11 measurements

Any light source can be measured and transferred into the rendering software via a Pythonbased transcoding script. This enables the rendering pipeline to be adapted to any curatorial requirement. In non-standard exhibition contexts-particularly for experimental films-curators may wish to recreate a specific analog viewing experience. Renderings can be calculated using any of these illuminants, chosen based on historical knowledge of a film's premiere screening, curatorial decisions, or intended distribution format-cinema, home theater, TV set, computer screen, or mobile device.

The rendering software includes four different color matching functions for standard observers 8 -Stockman-Sharpe 2° CMFs, Judd-Vos 2° CMFs, 9 CIE1964 10° CMFs and CIE1931 2° CMFs. 10 This choice makes it possible to test the results of different color vision models in laboratory settings where full control of the visualization pipeline is available. For use in conventional settings, CIE1931 2° CMFs should be selected. These decisions must be recorded and communicated in the metadata file in a human-readable form.

When transmittance spectra are sampled at intervals of 5 nm or less, the CIE recommends computing tristimulus values with the standard summations once an illuminant and an observer have been specified. For spectra of lower resolution-such as those obtained from a 10-band film scan-various deconvolution and interpolation methods have been proposed to refine the spectral interval and improve the accuracy of the resulting colorimetric values. However, these approaches often require a color target to achieve a meaningful improvement.

For each frame scanned with seven bands, fourteen uncompressed 16-bit images (seven per light geometry) with a resolution exceeding 4K generate a data volume of more than 420 MB. In the context of film scanning, where tens of thousands of such datasets may be produced, streamlining the computational pipeline becomes essential. To this end, we tested a more efficient color calculation method that, instead of upsampling the transmittance spectra, downsamples the illuminant and observer functions to align with the spectral bands. Once an illuminant and a standard observer are selected, the CIE recommends applying standard summations to compute the tristimulus values. This approach covers the range from 380 to 780

nanometers, with a step size of 1 nanometer. A detailed description of the color calculation is reported in a previous publication. 11

Depending on the intended viewing environment-such as an office, a living room, or a theater-the user can choose the most appropriate tonal response curve. For instance, a gamma of 2.6 is typically recommended for cinema projection, while a gamma of 2.2 has been used for the images presented in this paper.

## Style Transfer

Film digitization and restoration often face the challenge of combining different source elements-negatives, interpositives, internegatives, or projection prints-that vary in sharpness, dynamic range, and color rendering. Each type of element contributes distinct strengths: camera negatives usually provide the highest image quality and completeness, while exhibition prints more accurately reflect the color adjustments made for narrative functions, consistency, and aesthetic preferences.

Multi-sourced Aesthetic Transfer (MAT) addresses this challenge by transferring the color palette of a reference element (often an exhibition print) onto a higher-quality source scan (such as the camera negative). This process integrates structural fidelity with historically authentic color, ensuring technical quality and respecting the historical source material. 12

The workflow involves:

1. Selecting representative frame pairs from source and reference materials.
2. Capturing them with high-quality, color-accurate scanning methods.
3. Registering and aligning frames for pixel-to-pixel correspondence.
4. Generating look-up tables (LUTs) to minimize color differences-1D LUTs for straightforward cases, 3D LUTs for more complex color transformations.
5. Applying these LUTs in color grading software across the full film sequence.

In combination with multispectral film scanning, MAT offers a robust methodology to harmonize disparate film elements. The outcome is a digital rendering that balances aesthetic coherence, historical authenticity, and high technical quality-preserving films as they were intended to be experienced.

## Conclusion

A scientifically rigorous multispectral digitization and post-processing workflow offers a sustainable path for translating historical color films into the digital domain. This approach not only captures a detailed amount of spectral color information embedded in a film stock, but it also establishes a foundation for present and future renderings that aim to reconstruct a film's authentic color appearance on the cinema screen. By incorporating measurements of historical projection illuminants directly into the visual rendering software, the workflow enables consideration of diverse exhibition contexts. Accurately encoding the full spectrum of film colors-including those outside the gamut of current display technologies-ensures compatibility with future technological innovations such as multi-primary displays, wider color gamut, or other emerging standards. Finally, by producing a series of transmittance images for

each spectral band, the workflow remains device-independent and safeguards optimal sustainability for long-term storage, preservation, and continued access.

The digitization of existing content libraries, particularly non-digital physical media, is crucial for their long-term preservation and reuse. A significant challenge in this process, especially for historical film, is achieving accurate color reproduction and authenticity, which sometimes necessitates color correction after digitization to match the film's original release appearance.

To address this, a rigorously science-backed multispectral scanning workflow is utilized. This advanced method is essential because traditional scanners, with their limited spectral bands, often fail to capture the unique spectral characteristics of historical film colors, some of which fall outside current standard color spaces. Multispectral scanning, by employing a uniform distribution of spectral bands across the visible spectrum, directly extracts the inherent color information from historical film stocks. This material-based technology facilitates physically accurate rendering, with the ultimate goal of representing the color appearance as it would have been perceived on the cinema screen, thereby minimizing subjective interventions and upholding restoration ethics. The workflow integrates measurements of various historical cinema projection illuminants and employs colorimetric calculations with standard observers to compute color values directly from multispectral scans, eliminating the need for extensive, subjective color grading. This scientific methodology ensures transparency, sustainability, and reversibility, making the resulting digital elements future-proof and compatible with emerging display technologies.

This profound emphasis on color science also extends to advancements in modern color grading workflows, where it is being applied to automate the typically time-consuming and labor-intensive task of shot matching. Algorithms developed using color science and a colorist's approach focus on key aspects such as overall mood (color balance and exposure), faces, and objects, often incorporating machine learning techniques. Studies indicate that this automated approach can achieve approximately 70% of a colorist's grade while saving about 20% of the time, leading to a superior starting point and overall improved quality in less time. The output is intuitive and editable, offering control over balance, exposure, and flare.

## AI-Assisted Post-Production: Enhancing Workflows with AI Interpolation and Object Detection

Brian Gaffney, MTI FILM

## Written for presentation at the SMPTE 2025 Media and Technology Summit

## Abstract

AI-assisted methods are redefining workflows in post-production, enabling faster turnaround and more precise automation without sacrificing creative control. Recent advances in deep learning have produced practical solutions for long-standing technical challenges such as frame rate conversion, slate detection for dailies, and restoration of missing or damaged frames.

This paper presents technical details of three such applications: (1) the use of RIFE interpolation augmented by NVIDIA TensorRT for accurate AI-based frame rate conversion, (2) object detection using Ultralytics YOLOv11 for slate identification in dailies workflows, and (3) generative AI -based frame inference for restoration of archival film. Case studies -including the recent 4K restoration of Sunset Boulevard at USC -illustrate how targeted models trained on relevant datasets can accelerate creative processes in production and restoration while keeping human operators firmly in control.

## 1. Introduction

The convergence of artificial intelligence and traditional post-production has introduced new efficiencies to creative workflows. Beyond generative models for scene synthesis and storytelling, task-specific AI systems are now addressing long-standing bottlenecks in the technical domain. Video frame interpolation, intelligent object detection, and generative frame

reconstruction are three areas where measurable improvements are already being seen in production and restoration environments.

Rather than replacing human operators, these AI models function as assistive systems: automating tedious or repetitive tasks, reducing error-prone manual labor, and allowing artists and technicians to spend more time on higher-value quality control and creative decisionmaking.

This paper discusses three cornerstone technologies:

- AI-based frame rate conversion -powered by RIFE (Real-Time Intermediate Flow Estimation) and accelerated by NVIDIA TensorRT, enabling precise interpolation between frames for professional mastering and international delivery.
- AI object-based slate detection -fine-tuned Ultralytics YOLOv11 models trained to identify the 'slate clap' moment across dailies rolls, reducing manual search times.
- Generative AI frame inference for restoration -temporal and learned models that reconstruct missing or severely damaged frames in archival or degraded material.

## Examples from Submarine., Topkapi, and Designing Woman.

illustrate their application and reliability. These techniques demonstrate a new collaborative relationship between human artistry and machine intelligence in post-production.

## 2. AI Frame Interpolation with RIFE and TensorRT

Traditional optical flow interpolation is computationally expensive and often introduces artifacts, especially in scenes with fast lateral motion, occlusions, or complex lighting. RIFE, a deeplearning-based method for frame interpolation, uses dynamic attention mechanisms to estimate motion and synthesize intermediate frames with remarkable temporal coherence.

The challenge is to synthesize new frames but respect the time base, motion within a scene, light, reflections and all detail within the surrounding frames without generating undo artifacting.

At MTI FILM, we have integrated RIFE into our pipeline and optimized its inference time using NVIDIA's TensorRT runtime. TensorRT accelerates the execution of trained models on NVIDIA GPUs by converting PyTorch-based networks into a high-performance runtime format. Through precision calibration (FP16/INT8) and kernel fusion, we achieved real-time or faster-than-realtime frame interpolation for common frame rate conversions, such as:

- 23.976fps to 25fps for international delivery
- 29.97fps to 23.976fps for cinematic repurposing and UHD remastering

This solution powers the AI-based frame rate conversion , offering frame synthesis accuracy sufficient for professional-grade deliverables. The tool has been especially useful in restoring legacy broadcast material or preparing international masters without introducing cadence errors or ghosting.

## a. What is Video Frame Interpolation (VFI)?

VFI is the process of creating new frames to insert between existing ones in a video, effectively increasing the video's frame rate. This leads to smoother, more fluid motion, especially noticeable in slow-motion or fast-action sequences that exhibit high contrast, typical of digital cameras capturing at 23.98fps.

## b. How RIFE Works:

RIFE utilizes a neural network called IFNet to estimate the intermediate flow (motion) between frames. It then uses this flow information to synthesize new frames, essentially predicting where pixels should move from one frame to the next.

Unlike some other methods, RIFE doesn't rely on pre-trained optical flow models and can handle arbitrary time-step interpolation. MTI FILM integrated this model into an editing platform CORTEX, to allow all of the supported restoration file formats such as DPX, EXR, TIFF as well as ProRes and all camera supported codecs to be frame converted. This was the larger challenge, getting these tools to understand timecode and frame count and to maintain consistency across the time base of the source media.

This tool was designed to also work with IMF creations and supports DOLBY Vision 5.0 so that converted files can ingest the source XML containing the DOLBY Vision metadata and the synthesized media will create unique JSON files per clip that are concatenated into one file and reprocessed via DOLBY Metafier. This newly generated XML contains the updated frame converted cut points that match the new cut points. QC of the transforms proves the process works properly. This use case of AI assisted artists with MTai FrameConvert has been used successfully on major A-Title films since 2022.

## Example Video:

## Conversion Result Examples

## 3. Automated Slate Detection Using YOLOv11

One of the most time-consuming manual tasks for a dailies operator is identifying the precise frame when the film slate closes -critical for sound synchronization. One approach to address this is to use AI based Object Detection for model training . Using the finetuned Ultralytics'

YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once, version 11) object detection model using and a proprietary dataset of over 10,000 manually annotated frames containing slates in various positions and lighting conditions from various television productions and archives.

## The model detects:

- Slate presence
- Open vs. closed state
- Timecode metadata is detected using the Audio waveform metadata
- (No OCR is currently used) due to issues related to production

By integrating this into the AI based Object Detection module, the system searches for and tries to flag the exact "clap" frame across camera rolls, reducing manual search time from minutes to seconds with object detection.

Object detection is a task that involves identifying the location and class of objects in an image or video stream. The output of an object detector is a set of bounding boxes that enclose the objects in the image, along with class labels and confidence scores for each box. Object detection is a good choice when you need to identify objects of interest in a scene, but don't need to know exactly where the object is or its exact shape.


This AI-assisted solution is particularly beneficial in multi-cam environments or when metadata is incomplete or inconsistent. The tool enables operators to spend more time reviewing sync

quality instead of hunting for the correct frame of a closed slate. Frame accuracy is dependent on visibility as slates may not even appear in a frame during Wild Track or repeated takes.

The image below shows the flagged frame that the MTai SlateDetect, using the Yolov11 model, was trained on. Several training passes using well over 10,00 frames that were manually annotated as Open, Closed, or No-Slate so that the system could train and learn and produce a model that has been incorporated into commercial products for dailies. The system detects in milliseconds the slates and displays these detected marked slates as ORANGE for 'found slate' and GREEN for 'found closed slate' and RED 'found no slate' and this status assist the dailies operators QC process and allows them to vet the detection and confirm to auto-sync sound and picture of offset and accept to refine the AI detection. This process reduces the search and seek method of manual dailies and allows operators to further inspect the notes, comments, adjust for off-speed materials and any custom camera formats introduced as is often in a new show supporting dailies. Example Video

## 4. Restoration with Generative AI Frame Inference

Generative AI frame inference combines temporal modeling with edge-aware optical flow to reconstruct missing or unrepairable frames. This has proven invaluable in reviving archival footage where traditional manual or optical techniques are insufficient.

In collaboration with Paramount Pictures, this technique was used in the 2024 4K restoration of Sunset Boulevard . According to Charlotte Barker, Director of Restoration Services at Paramount, the process restored 14 instances of missing frames and jump cuts, while maintaining consistency in grain structure and character detail.

The system leverages GAN-refined synthesis steps to ensure results that are visually indistinguishable from neighboring frames during playback and grading. This technique extends beyond missing material to frames with extreme warping, water damage, raking, or other irreparable physical defects.

'Topkapi' - Courtesy Film Foundation - Tear replacement with MTai FrameGen and other tools


'Submarine' - Sony Picture Classis Frank Capra Collection - Unrepairable raking across frames


'Submarine' - Sony Picture Classis Frank Capra Collection - Repaired with AI Frame Generation


## Example Video

## 5. Results and Discussion

All three three of the listed AI cornerstone technologies share a design philosophy: AI should serve artists by reducing tedium, not replacing judgment. Key results include:

| Technology                      | Avg. Time Saved      | Accuracy        | Use Case                 |
|---------------------------------|----------------------|-----------------|--------------------------|
| AI-based Frame Rate Conversion  | 10x vs. optical flow | <1% frame error | 23.976 - 25fps mastering |
| AI Object-Based Slate Detection | 2 - 4 sec/clip       | >98% detection  | Sound sync for dailies   |

| GenAI Frame Inference for   | N/A (restoration)   | Artist-   | Missing/damaged   |
|-----------------------------|---------------------|-----------|-------------------|

## 6. Limitations and Quality Control

All content to be frame converted requires frame breaks or an EDL to let the RIFE interpolation model know that a new source should be loaded and interpolated and that the frame before was not contiguous to the new scene. These unmarked events can cause unwanted "hallucinations" with the interpolation. This occurs primarily on:

- Lateral Motion on a scene break
- When Source detail is only existing for one frame
- Tends to occur on breaks at the beginning and end of scenes

Various applications can perform automatic shot detection but ideally an EDL or XML file are provided to provide an exact reference.

QC is required and when a hallucination is generated, the system provides the ability to playback both frame rates simultaneously, in sync, and allows for full frame replacement from the source or the ability to paint within a frame to correct any aberrations.

Providing an ability to correct the AI assist is critical and another example of why AI tools won't replace artists but rather assist them in providing a better restored product. See below, a 23.98 and 29.97 source can be viewed and played in sync and frames painted or replaced with a simple shift-insert command or in frame painting process.


The frame on the right shows distortion caused by AI Interpolation on lateral movement. Especially when breaking frame and entering from off axis can cause a frame or two of distortion that needs to be replaced using AI restoration tools such as Paint and Frame replacement techniques

## 7. Conclusion and Future Work

AI is proving its value across post-production tasks -when trained and deployed correctly. In practice, AI-assisted artistry enables operators to remain in creative control while reducing technical burdens.

Future development will focus on:

- Expanding generative frame inference for noise reduction and flicker correction
- Enhancing object detection for QC tasks (e.g., boom mics, crew reflections, signage)
- Investigating diffusion-based inpainting for gate hair and fine-grain restoration

AI will not replace artists -but it will redefine their workflows, providing an assistive layer that extends human capability.

## From Captions to Translations: Evaluating Readiness for AI-Powered Live Language Solutions

## Bill McLaughlin, Chief Product Officer,


## Cody Farenga, MBA, Director of Global Training & Quality


## Cody Parnell, Manager of Global Training & Quality, North America


## Written for presentation at the

## SMPTE 2025 Media and Technology Summit

Abstract . As artificial intelligence reshapes live media workflows, the focus of new projects in language and localization is entering a new phase - shifting from same-language AI captioning to new applications for real-time language translation. This paper discusses the merits of the Number Translation Recognition (NTR) metric for evaluating translations, and investigates through this metric whether the performance trajectory of low latency automated translation is on track to follow the same path of rapid improvement seen in the similar Number Edition Recognition (NER) scores commonly used to measure the accuracy of same language captioning.

We begin with a comparative analysis of NER and NTR metrics at similar stages of model maturity. Drawing on historical NER data - where captioning accuracy has steadily improved from 97 - 97.5% in 2021 to 98.5 - 99% in 2025 - we present early NTR evaluation data and identify parallel performance patterns. We argue that, like NER, NTR can benefit from structured evaluation frameworks that enable clear benchmarking and drive iterative model development.

Building on this foundation, the paper explores the operational implications of growth in AI captioning quality, including advances in model evaluation and analytics workflows. Through the use of AI-Media's LEXI (AI captioning) and LEXI Voice (AI translation) platforms as applied use cases, we analyze how structured evaluation datasets and feedback loops enable rapid iteration and measurable quality improvements across AI-based language products.

Finally, the paper proposes a framework for evaluating industry readiness to adopt AI-powered live translation as a production-standard solution. This framework considers technical performance benchmarks, workflow integration, and operational preparedness - providing practical guidance for broadcasters, content owners, and live event producers seeking to expand reach through multilingual

delivery.

Keywords. AI captioning, AI translation, NER, NTR, live automatic captions, live translation, speech recognition, machine translation, text-to-speech (TTS), large language models (LLMs), voice synthesizer, evaluation metrics, structured datasets, broadcast accessibility, multilingual delivery, real-time media workflows, quality benchmarking, iterative model development, workflow integration, operational readiness, compounding AI workflows

## Introduction

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming live media workflows across a broad spectrum of problems. In natural language AI, technologies that were cutting edge a decade ago, such as automatic speech to text captioning for regulated live television programs, have become commonplace. Today, innovations in natural language AI for live media are pressing beyond automated same-language captioning into real-time multilingual translation, delivered either as text captions or paired with text-to-speech AI for fully synthesized audio tracks. These AI-driven solutions can serve as a substitution for the original language, replacing it entirely for distribution to a new audience, or as supplementary layer, expanding audience reach and accessibility. As AI powered media translations become increasingly available and inexpensive, a key question arises: Will translation systems in the next several years achieve accuracy improvements on the same rapid trajectory achieved by captioning systems in the past several years, and achieve the quality level re quired for widespread commercial use?

To investigate this question, we will need to begin by discussing quantification of translation accuracy and how to effectively compare metrics of same language captioning quality to those assessing the more complex question of translation quality.

In live same-language captioning, accuracy and quality is frequently measured by the NER model (Number, Edition, Recognition) - a standard that considers a variety of inconsistencies and error types to calculate an accuracy percentage. The NER system is somewhat more subjective than a simple WER (word error rate) percentage but aims for a better representation of the varying impact of different error types on reader comprehension. Errors that render phrases nonsensical or change the meaning materially are strongly penalized, while some small phrasing discrepancies could be labelled only as minor errors or immaterial.

A target of 98% NER accuracy has been established in many broadcast accessibility guidelines, as well as in legally binding regulations in some countries (Romero-Fresco & Van Gauwbergen, 2025, Sec.6.1). Live captions from highly qualified human captioners regularly achieve 98.9 to 99.5% scores, while AI-systems have steadily closed the gap since commercial adaption began in the early 2010s. Recent NER evaluations of AI-Media's LEXI ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition) captioning, for example, found average 2025 accuracy scores around 99% in English. We will present historical NER findings from the last 3 years within this study.

This paper examines whether live AI translations can be effectively measured with a similar system developed by the same authors called NTR - (Number, Translation, Recognition), and whether early results can shed light on the readiness of these systems for commercial adoption and the current pace of improvement. Initial NTR evaluations show promising accuracy levels (~98.5-98.9%) that already match same language live captioning benchmarks from only two years prior, suggesting AI translation readiness and adoption may progress at least as quickly as AI captioning already has.

We further explore how structured evaluation frameworks and interconnected AI workflows accelerate these quality metrics. Drawing on three years of NER data and early NTR findings, we present a framework for assessing readiness to adopt AI translation at scale. Our analysis also touches on the workflow integration and operational considerations needed to bring live AI translation into production environments. By demonstrating that translation accuracy is rapidly approaching captioning levels, we argue that the industry may be on the cusp of a new era of instant and automatic localization - where real-time AI translation becomes a core and accepted component of live media delivery.

## Data-Driven Iteration: The Role of Structured Evaluation

A crucial driver behind the constant quality improvements in AI captioning and translation is the use of structured evaluation datasets and metrics. Rather than relying on anecdotal feedback, AI language systems are measured on standardized tests at each iteration. The NER and NTR evaluation frameworks represent this approach. Each provides a quantifiable score that captures a model's performance on representative content, allowing developers to track progress over time and identify particular error types. Figures 2 and 3 define the formulas used for each evaluation model. For instance, AI-Media analyzes thousands of hours of content to calculate NER accuracy across diverse programs. Consistent evaluations revealed that the

newest LEXI release continuously delivered ~98.9% accuracy on varied content, up to ~99.5% in certain areas. (AI-Media, n.d.)

Figure 2. Number Edition Recognition (NER) Formula

## Where:

- N : Total number of words

- E

- : Edition errors

- R : Recognition errors

Figure 3. Number Translation Recognition (NTR) Formula

## Where:

- R : Recognition errors

These evaluations provide required compliance data for regulated customers and inform rollout decisions for various programs and languages, while also creating a feedback loop for engineers developing future versions of the system. By examining the errors contributing to the remaining ~1-2%, the development team can pinpoint weaknesses (e.g. names, punctuation, dialectical speech, presence of background sounds), and then fine tune the model or add data to correct and address the errors. In fact, each release has drastically reduced specific error categories: one recent version showed up to 60% fewer recognition and formatting errors than prior generations (AI-Media, n.d.). These improvements were achieved by studying the breakdown of NER scores before and after model updates - proving how these evaluations tailor iterative improvements.

Applying this philosophy to live translation is even more important, as there is a greater diversity of ways errors can arise - for example, errors propagated from misunderstandings in the original language, those that come from incomplete context in a translated phrase unit, those that come from transfer of idiomatic or unusual phrases, or those that come from fundamental issues between certain language pairs such as differences in use of speaker or object gender or in use of tone and formality.

If testing reveals a decline in quality from a new version, developers can inspect to find patterns, whether these are incorrectly formatted numbers or idioms translated too literally. This datadriven approach was not always standard in traditional translation workflows, but AI development requires it. Comparative scoring allows rapid iteration development: small algorithm adjustments or added vocabulary can be verified in hours across thousands of sample sentences. Over time, this drives an efficient cycle of base accuracy improvement while also suggesting implementation best practices. For instance, additions to a channel-specific custom dictionary or glossary could be targeted to boost accuracy for a particular domain (e.g. news or sports broadcasts) if the evaluations show errors occurring mostly on niche content-specific terms.

In summary, structured datasets and quality metrics are key contributors of rapid AI iterative development. By using NER and NTR evaluations not just as report cards and marketing collateral, but as diagnostic tools, organizations can enhance their development cycle. Over time, groups of evaluations yield actionable data, and as we move forward, these frameworks will continue to drive advancement, ensuring that each iteration of any AI is objectively better than the last, to deliver accurate and reliable language output.

## Comparative Performance of AI Captioning vs. Translation

To understand the trajectory of AI-powered translation, it is important to compare it with the wellestablished recent progress of AI same language captioning. Figure 4 shows the accuracy trend of AI captioning from 2023 to 2025 alongside preliminary data from AI translation in 2025, while Figure 5 displays baseline descriptions anchored to what NER/NTR scores represent in terms of quality.

The starting basis for this comparison on the captioning side is the release of the Ai-Media Lexi 3.0 product in 2023, which used a new generation of underlying ASR models that would benefit strongly from the worldwide growth in investment and generalized performance of LLM (Large Language Model) based AI. At launch, NER evaluations showed this system performing with an average score of 98.5%, already a significant improvement over many past ASR captioning systems. As the models and surrounding software continued to improve, regular evaluations reached 98.75% in early 2024, then to 98.9% in late 2024, and over 99% in 2025. This rapid rise in capabilities has average measurements of the AI system exceeding those of many individual professional human service providers, and very consistently falling within the 'good' to 'excellent' range (98.5-99%+) defined for broadcast captions (Romero-Fresco & Van Gauwbergen, 2025, Sec.4.0-5.1).

Figure 4. Accuracy improvements in AI captioning vs. translation (NER vs. NTR).


Figure 5. NER/NTR Score Descriptions

Taking as the beginning for the NTR graph as the release of a similar generational improvement of the Lexi Translate service in April 2025, the performance of the translate service is lower than that of a same language captioning service today, but appears to be improving at the same rate or faster than the earlier system did at a comparable stage of development. When LEXI Voice live-translation was launched in April 2025, the early NTR scores were ~98.5%, on par with LEXI's same-language caption accuracy two years prior. NTR scores climbed to ~98.85% for English-to-Other language translation in August 2025.These results highlight a promising trend: despite the increased theoretical difficulty of the language translation task, AI translations in live

media may quickly reach the high accuracy range that is currently seen with same-language captions.

In addition to our internal system results, an external case study, Quality Assessment of Interlingual YouTube Auto-generated CCs , completed by Allam (Allam, 2023), applied the NTR model to auto-generated translations in analogous settings. In 2023, Allam evaluated autogenerated translated closed captions on YouTube and reported NTR accuracy rates of ~95% rising to 97.3% in just 9 months. This external case study, validates this approach and suggests similar trends in error rates that have been occurring even before the time period covered in our study.

Translation evaluation is more complex than same-language transcription, involving nuances of tone, fluency and idioms. NTR seeks to account for these factors by prioritizing the concept of whether key meaning is lost, rather than systems like BLEU which only give favorable scores to translations that use the exact same words as a canonical reference translation. Penalties are also assessed for issues with style and grammar when these issues are significant enough to impair understanding, or to confuse or distract the target audience.

Figure 6 details different NTR error categories and the associated scoring penalties.

The NTR model addresses idioms, tone, and fluency discrepancies via form-style errors, which are variations in appropriateness, naturalness and register of text that can be generated by poor choice of language or failing to maintain one style of text and instead mixing informal with formal text.

Consider the following example:


Could you please be quiet a moment?


Cállate. (Shut up)

The appropriateness, naturalness and register of the source text has been altered in the translation. Form-style errors are common within translations and depending on the severity, can change the meaning of the intended message. This example would be graded as a Critical error, as it completely changes the tone and naturalness of the source text.

Less severe form-style error:


Good afternoon, Britain. It's 1:00 on Friday the 14th of February.


Buenas tardes, Gran Bretaña. Es la 1:00 del viernes 14 de febrero.

This is an example of a minor form-style error. In Spanish, time is often expressed using the 24hour format.

Idiomatic expressions - another form-style error categorization:


It's raining cats and dogs.


Lueve a cántaros.

This is another critical form-style error, as the translation is a literal translation of the common expression 'It's raining cats and dogs'.

It is important that the NTR addresses idioms and naturalness, as these errors can drastically change the meaning of a translation.

Despite these complexities, NTR and NER are calibrated with the goal of producing similar scores for similar levels of subjective quality and usability. In the domain of media translation, it is reasonable to assume that NTR scores could approach but would not exceed NER scores for similar content, because a need to accurately transcribe the original source audio is a necessary subcomponent of a system that then goes on to translate to another language and represent the translated language as subtitles or as a new voice track. A corollary to this is that as NER scores and transcription accuracy in a source language improves, NTR scores will also improve as a more accurate base transcription leads to a more accurate translation. Independent evaluations confirm that cascade speech translation performance is tightly coupled to the accuracy of the speech recognition front-end (Tran, Thulke, Gao, Herold, & Ney, 2022). This compounding effect is a key factor accelerating the improvements of NTR evaluations.
