## Interconnected AI Workflows and Compounding Gains

An overarching theme in our findings is that AI captioning and translation do not develop in isolation, rather, they form an interconnected channel, where improvements in one AI component boosts the performance of the next. At its core, live ASR translation is built on the output of live captioning. The workflow resembles a set of essential constituents - first, an ASR

engine converts spoken audio into same-language captions; next, a machine translation engine converts those captions into a target language; finally, a text-to-speech (TTS) synthesizer can voice the translated text back to audio delivery, completing the cycle.

Figure 7. Interconnected Workflow Diagram


The nature of this design benefits from advances in individual components. For instance, when the underlying ASR captioning accuracy is improved by reducing transcription errors, the translation engine is interpreting a more accurate source language - thus improving translation accuracy even without any direct change to the AI translation engine.

While many advocate for end-to-end or joint models to avoid the cascaded approach, recent studies suggest that the performance gap between cascaded and end-to-end speech translation systems has become marginal. Bentivogli et al. (2021) carried out a thorough comparison of cascade vs direct speech translation across multiple language pairs using both automatic metrics and professional human post -edits. In essence, Bentivogli (2021) found that, 'the performance gap has effectively closed, with differences so modest they neither distinguish nor carry a clear preference in human evaluation.' This reinforces the argument in favor of modular, cascaded pipeline - especially where they already deliver strong base performance and where each component is a valuable additional output in the overall workflow. Other studies from Martucci et al. (2021), Etchegoyhen et al. (2022), and the National Institute of Communication Technology (2024) all found similar findings. These findings further reinforce the practicality and resilience of modular cascaded architectures, especially in real-world scenarios.

Significantly, this component-based architecture also drives innovation - developers do not need to build an all-in-one translation system from the ground up. Instead, they can leverage the best AI services for each workflow component. In many cases, different LLMs or machine translation engines are deployed for different languages, selecting whichever model has demonstrated the best performance for that language pair (Jacob, 2024). This could mean using separate vendors, for example the commercial AI-Media system tested may use Google for one language pair and DeepL for another based on prior testing results. As new and improved models become available, they can be integrated into the process, presenting their benefits to the live translation workflow.

There is NTR and research evidence that supports this pick-and-choose model approach. Recent work by Meta AI and Licht et al. (2022) demonstrated substantial variability in human evaluation expectations and quality scores across 14 language pairs. Their findings indicate that

human evaluators bring different implicit standards depending on the target and source pairs, and other exposures. This finding supports the necessity, in our NTR and caption translation settings, to report performance separately by language pair, especially for metrics beyond raw accuracy, such as idioms, meaning preservation, and other factors. In short, different language pairings can introduce further complexities which can influence industry adoption, which is why performing NTR evaluations across these varying engines and language pairs is crucial.

So, what factors have an impact on this interconnected workflow? The compounding gains manifest in many ways:

1. Accuracy synergy : Less errors in the ASR stage prevent error propagation downstream. It is known that ASR errors can cascade into eventual translation errors, so reducing their frequency helps the translations immensely (Tran et al., 2022, p.3).
2. Efficiency and development speed : Developers begin from a high baseline (previous components) rather than zero. For example, when building LEXI Voice, by making use of LEXI AI captions as an input, product development for AI translation was accelerated, as one of the most significant challenges (accurate same-language ASR captions) had been largely resolved. This lowers the operational threshold for deploying new capabilities, and reduces technical friction for scaling live translations.
3. Rapid cross-domain improvements : Improvements in general AI research are fed into the workflow. An example is the recent boost in AI voice synthesis. New TTS (Text To Speech) technologies, such as ElevenLabs' voice-cloning, can now generate speech in multiple languages while preserving the original speaker's vocal characteristics (Eleven Labs, 2023).

In parallel, what factors have an impact on NTR score increases and what changes have historically caused scores to improve in the past?:

1. NTR Model Adoption Growth : Unlike the NER model, which is broadly recognized across broadcasters and regulators globally, the NTR model is relatively new, as mass translation of content is still being adopted (Korybski, Davitti, Orăsan, & Braun, 2022). As a result, many NTR evaluators are still learning how to apply the model. Luckily, similarities between the models means evaluators already trained in NERs can quickly familiarize themselves with the NTR process. However, the NTR model requires fluency in both languages under evaluation, where the number of trained multilinguists is limited.
2. Voice Quality : NTR quality scores only measure correctness in translation, not how natural and appropriate the voice sounds in a system where the ultimate output is audio. However, TTS research shows that voice systems are improving fast. Modern models are progressing and can closely mimic tones, nuances in pacing, and even slight hesitations - all details that enhance naturalness and commercial utility but fall outside traditional NTR scoring. A thorough evaluation for a given commercial purpose would include these factors as well, in much the same way that evaluation of a captioning service may also include non-NER factors such as visual positioning and reading speed.
3. Historical Improvement : Several key aspects explain the steady rise in ASR captioning accuracy, including better data, custom models and vocabulary, and faster iterative development. Modern ASR systems now benefit from massive datasets, including training methods using unlabeled data, enabling them to improve in areas like accent diversity and specialized vocabulary. Features, like the ability to upload custom topic models, including

industry-specific or branded terminology, helps improve recognition dramatically. And lastly, developers can now rapidly test, evaluate, and tune models using standardized metrics, like NER and NTR, contributing to accuracy gains. As the adoption of AI translation models continues, and available datasets increase, we can expect to see similar improvements in translation accuracy as a result of the same virtuous cycle of larger and more diverse data, domain-specific customization, and rapid model iteration that has already transformed ASR.

## Readiness for AI-Powered Live Translation: Framework and Outlook

With the technical foundations rapidly bedding down, we turn to the big question about market readiness. How prepared are broadcasters, streamers, and live event producers to adopt realtime, AI translation as a standard solution?

To demonstrate readiness, we have included two pilot case studies in varying media environments, including our internal data. Allam (2023) involves auto-generated translated closed captions on YouTube and Alonso-Bacigulpe (2023) involves simultaneous interpretation and live subtitling tasks evaluated with NTR in academic/public settings. These illustrate how the workflow integration challenges operate in different production environments.

Below is a proposed framework of key considerations to evaluate readiness, encompassing performance benchmarks, workflow integration, and operational factors:

1. Technical Performance Benchmarks : Determining whether AI translation meets the quality bar for professional use will always be the primary focus, though no global benchmark has been established. However, stakeholders must consider use-case complexities, such as; does the system maintain accuracy for unscripted, fast dialogue, or heavy use of idioms? Are there certain language pairs with lower performance? Considering these factors, readiness assessments can be applied to AI translation on applicable contenttypes (news/sports/events/enterprise/etc.). If the AI model can consistently deliver intelligible, accurate translations, then the technical benchmark is met. In summary, this technology is approaching readiness. We expect that by maintaining structured evaluations and continued iterative development, as described in Section 2, remaining quality gaps will continue to shrink.
2. Workflow Integration : Another vital consideration of readiness for deployment is how well the AI solution fits into existing AI and technology workflows. Live captioning and translation systems must ingest audio and video feeds, generate captions, translate them, and output said captions and/or audio in the desired language(s) - all within a live program workflow. With broadcasting, this means the AI translation model should integrate with caption encoders, streaming platforms, or even in-venue display systems; and should interface via standard video/audio protocols, for example SMPTE 2110, SRT, and SDI. Industry readiness for AI translation depends on how seamlessly these systems integrate into existing broadcast workflows.
3. Scalability and Redundancy : The system should scale to multiple languages or events, and have fail-safes (like Disaster Recovery) in case of any AI issues. When evaluating

readiness, organizations should conduct pilot programs to ensure the AI translation can be inserted into their live workflow, without causing major delays or requiring excessive manual intervention. Successful trials by early adopters suggest that integration is achievable with today's technology, often requiring minimal configuration and testing. Moreover, this approach presents advantages over the current human-based model, where scaling to multiple languages or venues often requires large teams of interpreters, significant logistical coordination, and limited redundancy. By contrast, AI translation can be deployed instantly across channels, with built-in disaster recovery options that reduce operational risk and cost.

4. Operations Preparedness : The final aspect involves human and organizational factors. Even the best AI products require operation and monitoring. For example, staff training to manage AI captioning or translation during a live event, knowing how to configure language pairs, adding custom vocabulary, and knowing how to handle errors. Operational readiness also means setting up quality control, including having bilingual monitors review samples of the output (NER and NTR evaluations), especially during early adoption, to verify accuracy and pick up any systemic issues. Over time, as confidence in AI translation and voice grows, the level of oversight can be reduced, as seen with same-language captioning. However, initially, a hybrid approach is prudent.
5. Commercial Readiness : Technical capability alone does not ensure adoption - it must translate into audience engagement and revenue. AI translation goes beyond accessibility, unlocking new opportunities for global reach, market expansion, and monetization.
- Audience Need: 80% of global content is inaccessible to non-native speakers. Billions of people speak only 12 major languages.
- Revenue Upside: For broadcasters, language barriers mean lost viewers, limited influence, and missed advertising and subscription opportunities.
- Market Drivers: Regulatory pressure and internal DE&I mandates push organizations towards inclusive communication.
- Operational Gains: AI translations and synthetic voice improve efficiency, reduce resourcing, and standardize workflows.
- Expansion: Global expansion and reach into new markets, boosting engagement both in-premise and online.
- Viewer Experience: Enhances the viewer experience and perceived production value.
- Advertising and Licensing: Creates new advertising opportunities with multilingual spots, and opens licensing and syndication through localization.
- Subscriptions: Drives subscription and streaming revenue through multilingual offerings.
6. Benchmarks to Outcomes : One key question remains - how do NTR scores map into audience and commercial outcomes? While 98% accuracy is an established benchmark for captioning, the 'breaking point' for translation quality - where viewers disengage versus embrace AI translation - has not been studied in sufficient detail. As the NTR model adoption increases, future studies will need to link accuracy metrics with outcomes such as audience retention, engagement, advertising performance, and subscription growth, ensuring that technical progress directly translates into business impact.

## AI Translation Adoption: A Prediction

In evaluating all of these factors, the trend is clearly moving toward adoption. Market indicators show a growing confidence in AI translation. A recent industry analysis predicted that over 75% of businesses offering global services will integrate AI speech translation tools by the end of 2025, reflecting the increasing trust and demand for this technology (KUDO, 2025).

## Conclusion - A Roadmap for Adoptions

In summary, our research suggests that AI-powered live translation is positioned to follow the same success path as AI captioning, only faster . The early evidence of NTR evaluations, combined with other evaluation practices and the power of interconnected AI products, is

accelerating towards a new era in live media. To fully realize this potential, industry stakeholders should adopt a systematic framework; verify the AI's performance against quality benchmarks, confirm smooth integration into workflows, and prepare their teams and processes for an AI-guided environment. With these principles, broadcasters and content creators can confidently expand their global reach through multilingual delivery, leveraging AI to break down language barriers in real time. The compounding gains of AI workflows, where one system's output shapes another's input, will continue to drive innovation, making live translation more accurate, scalable, and efficient. By building on the strong foundation of AI captioning, the media industry in 2025 is ready to embrace AI-powered live translation as a standard part of production, opening the door to a truly global audience.

## Abstract

Artificial intelligence is becoming central to live media workflows, powering real-time object tracking, automated replay generation, camera switching, and personalized viewing experiences. These applications demand extremely low latency and efficient use of compute and network resources. Existing mezzanine formats such as JPEG 2000 and ProRes were designed for human viewing, not machine inference. They require full-frame decoding and multiple transcoding stages, which add delay, duplicate processing, and inflate infrastructure costs as AI workloads scale.

This paper introduces VC6, a hierarchical, region-aware codec standardized as SMPTE ST 2117-1, and demonstrates its integration with swXtch.io's AI-native multicast networking to enable selective, AI-ready live video transport. Unlike traditional codecs, VC6 supports multiresolution Levels of Quality (LOQ) and region-of-interest (ROI) decoding, allowing AI models to access only the portions of a frame needed for inference. When combined with swXtch.io's multicast overlay, a single VC6 stream can serve multiple models in parallel without redundant encodes or proxy pipelines.

Benchmark testing on NVIDIA RTX A6000 and Intel i9-13900K systems shows up to 73% faster decoding compared to CUDA JPEG, 20× faster preprocessing when scaling is integrated into decode, and approximately 10× lower encode/decode complexity than JPEG 2000. Live

multicast evaluations confirm predictable low latency even when multiple AI workloads run concurrently from a shared source.

By moving preprocessing intelligence into the transport layer, the combined VC6 and swXtch.io architecture creates a practical foundation for scalable, energy-efficient, and standardscompliant AI-native live video workflows. This work represents the first implementation of a SMPTE-standardized hierarchical codec directly aligned with AI inference pipelines, offering a pathway for future interoperability within ST 2110 and related IP media ecosystems.

Keywords : VC6, SMPTE ST 2117-1, AI-native networking, multicast, region-of-interest decoding, live video workflows, preprocessing acceleration

## Top Three Learning Takeaways

1. How a hierarchical, region-aware data format changes the cost and latency profile of live AI preprocessing.
2. How multicast transport with VC-6 enables many AI workloads to share one source without proxy pipelines.
3. How to integrate VC-6 and swXtch.io with platforms like NVIDIA Holoscan and Triton in cloud or hybrid deployments.

## Type of Paper

Novel Technological Approaches

## Target Audience

Broadcast engineers, AI and ML developers for media, live production workflow designers, cloud media architects, and technologists focused on compression and transport optimization.

## 1. Introduction

## 1.1 The AI shift in live media

Live production is moving into a phase where AI is no longer an afterthought. Sports broadcasts, live news coverage, esports tournaments, and corporate events are embedding models directly in the signal path. Object detection, instant replay generation, camera switching, and automated overlays must run with minimal delay. The infrastructure that feeds those models was built for human viewing rather than machine inference. Full-frame decoding,

multiple transcoding stages, cropping and redundant network transport add latency and inflate compute costs.

## 1.2 Why the transport layer matters

AI performance is often judged by model speed and accuracy, but the path data takes to reach the model can be just as important. In live environments, video is frequently duplicated and reencoded to create model-specific versions. Each extra copy burns CPU and GPU cycles, increases cloud egress, and adds latency. These duplications show up directly in the utilization and latency metrics summarized in Section 4. By rethinking the transport layer, the link between acquisition and inference, it is possible to eliminate redundant work and feed models in a way that makes better use of available compute.

## 1.3 The role of VC-6 with swXtch.io

V Nova VC-6 and swXtch.io AI-native networking work together to solve this problem. VC-6 uses a hierarchical, region-aware structure that lets a model request only the part of a frame it needs at the quality level that fits the task. The swXtch.io multicast overlay delivers that data directly to AI consumers without proxy servers or additional transcoding. The network becomes an active part of preprocessing. Video is shaped for AI while it moves, and many AI workflows can share a single encoded stream in real time.

## 2. VC-6 Technical Overview

VC-6 is standardized as SMPTE ST 2117-1 and is a fully intra-frame codec built for high speed, selective access to visual data. Unlike codecs designed only for human consumption, VC-6 is structured to match the way AI processes images.

The codec organizes each frame into multiple levels of quality, which store progressively higher resolution detail. Applications can retrieve a low-resolution version for quick processing or a high-resolution version for detailed analysis without decoding and fetching the entire frame. The same structure supports region of interest decoding and retrieval, so a model can request a specific section of the image, for example a player's location on a sports field, without touching or sending the rest of the pixels.

VC-6 also supports multi-plane encoding, which means it can store separate channels for luma, chroma, and alpha or mask data. This is useful in AI pipelines that need segmentation maps or that generate graphics overlays alongside the video. Because the codec is designed for parallel decoding, it scales well on GPUs and can produce thumbnails in less than a millisecond.

## 3. Integration with swXtch.io AI Native Networking

SwXtch.io AI-native networking incorporates VC-6 in the network layer, so that video is prepared for AI consumption as it moves. The process starts at the swXtch AI Gateway, which ingests an ST 2110 feed and encodes it into VC-6 while also making the native ST 2110 signal available for traditional production workflows.

The encoded stream is delivered using the VC-6 MC protocol, an RTP over multicast transport that lets each AI consumer subscribe only to the level of quality or the regions it needs. This multicast distribution means that one VC-6 stream can serve many AI models in parallel, each receiving different subsets of the data without creating redundant encodes.

## ROI and LOQ request sequence

1. An AI model sends an ROI or LOQ request to the MCP server.
2. The MCP updates multicast subscription parameters for that consumer.
3. The swXtch.io AI Gateway delivers only the requested packets via VC-6 MC.
4. The AI model receives targeted frames and processes them immediately.

Sending native ST 2110 to each AI node would require full uncompressed streams and duplicate bandwidth for every consumer. VC-6 MC enables all nodes to pull selectively from the same compressed multicast without re-encoding. Because video shaping happens in the network, there is no need for a proxy layer to resize or crop content for different AI tasks. The result is a live AI pipeline with lower latency, reduced compute demand, and more predictable performance across multiple workloads.

## 4. Performance Benchmarking

Lab testing on GPU compared the CUDA implementation of VC-6 against NVIDIA's nvImageCodec formats (JPEG, JPEG 2000). Results show that VC-6 achieves shorter decode times while also supporting selective decoding at lower resolutions that more closely match AI model input requirements. This reduces unnecessary preprocessing steps such as full decode and rescale, lowering overall latency and compute demand.

Figure 1 summarises the results, obtained on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 using the DIV2K dataset at 2K resolution.


In addition to JPEG and JPEG 2000 lab tests, VC-6 was benchmarked against uncompressed ST 2110 transport at 1080p30 4:2:2 10-bit in a live multicast scenario. The results highlight several areas of improvement, while guaranteeing a comparable AI inference accuracy:

- Network Efficiency : VC-6 reduced average bandwidth from 1304 Mb/s to 89.7 Mb/s (93%) and packet rates from ~118k to ~8.1k packets per second (-96%). This reduction lowers network utilization, reduces interrupt overhead on receivers, and decreases cloud egress costs.
- Decode and Processing Time : Receive-side processing latency (decode time) for ST 2110 measured 32 ms per frame. VC-6 achieved 16.4 ms at LoQ-0 (-50%) and 9.6 ms at LoQ-2 (-70%), accelerating the delivery of model-ready frames and directly improving pipeline responsiveness.
- Transmission Path : End-to-end transmit processing for VC-6 averaged 30.9 ms per frame, comparable to 32.2 ms for ST 2110. These results were obtained with VC-6 encoding running on CPU, specifically on Intel Xeon Gold 6138 processors (20 cores). In practice, shifting the encode stage to GPU would further reduce processing overhead and deliver a more efficient end-to-end workflow, while still sustaining one order of magnitude lower bandwidth and packet load compared to ST 2110.
- End-to-End AI Latency : VC-6 reduced overall latency when lower Levels of Quality were used. At LoQ-0, mean latency was 731 ms, at LoQ-1 mean latency fell to 379 ms, and at LoQ-2 to 317 ms, cutting inference delays by more than half while preserving tracking performance. This provides operators with a practical trade-off between

resolution and responsiveness depending on workload requirements.

Live multicast tests confirmed low and predictable latency even when the same source served multiple AI workloads. Parallel fan-out to different models did not introduce measurable delays, which shows that selective decode and network-level distribution scale effectively. Detailed datasets, full methodology, and network environment are described in Appendix A.

## 5. Live AI Workflow Architecture

A live VC-6 and swXtch.io workflow begins with video capture in ST 2110. The swXtch AI Gateway encodes the signal into VC-6 and sends it over the cloudSwXtch multicast overlay. In the cloud, AI inference nodes subscribe directly to the multicast stream, while the original ST 2110 signal remains available for production use.

From this single source, multiple AI workloads can run in parallel. One model may track objects, another may assemble replay clips, and another may generate real-time overlays. Each pulls only the pixels and resolution it needs, which reduces the amount of data that moves through the pipeline.

Figure 2. VC-6 with swXtch.io live architecture


Figure 2 illustrates ground-to-cloud capture, VC-6 encoding, multicast distribution, and AI fanout. Because the same VC-6 stream serves all AI consumers, the design avoids the encoding duplication and network oversubscription that often limit scale in multi-model live workflows. The architecture is compatible with NVIDIA Holoscan for Media, Triton Inference Server, and a wide range of open source and commercial vision models. It can run in a single cloud or in a hybrid deployment where capture happens on premises and AI runs in the cloud.

## 6. Use Cases Enabled

## 6.1 Real-time object tracking with ROI based decoding

In most live AI setups, object tracking decodes the full frame even if the model only needs a small part of the image. This wastes compute and adds avoidable delay. With VC-6, a model can request only the region it needs at a matching resolution. The swXtch.io multicast network delivers that targeted data in parallel with other requests, so multiple models can track different objects at the same time without competing for bandwidth. This can reduce per-frame decode

data volume by up to 90 percent for typical tracking windows, for example a 640 by 480 region from a 3840 by 2160 source.

## 6.2 Sports highlight generation and replay assembly

Traditional highlight workflows clip from a full-resolution archive or ingest stream, which adds latency and storage overhead. VC-6 allows clips to be generated directly from the live multicast by decoding only the relevant time segment and level of quality. This enables automated replay assembly in seconds with lower CPU and GPU demand, making it practical to run multiple highlight pipelines at once. In tests, this reduced clip turnaround from 10 to 15 seconds to under 2 seconds.

## 6.3 Personalized viewports and zoomed feeds at the edge

Delivering personalized camera views usually means creating separate high-resolution encodes for each variant, which does not scale in live scenarios. With VC-6 multi-resolution layers, a single multicast stream can serve all variants. Edge nodes or client devices subscribe only to the viewports and quality levels they need. This reduces bandwidth, lowers cloud egress, and allows personalization to scale to large audiences without re-encoding, delivering up to 70 percent bandwidth savings compared to multiple high-resolution encodes.

## 6.4 Multi-task AI processing from a single source

Many live AI workflows run serially. A model processes the feed, hands off its output, and the next model starts. This serial structure adds delay and can become a bottleneck. VC-6 over swXtch.io supports a parallel model where detection, tracking, segmentation, and graphics generation all run at the same time from the same source stream. Each model works at the resolution and region it needs, which minimizes redundant processing and improves throughput. This design supports four or more simultaneous AI tasks with no increase in source encoding load.

## 6.5 Agentic AI network control

As AI becomes more autonomous, the ability to request data dynamically becomes important. The MCP server in the swXtch.io platform lets models monitor network state, query available streams, and request specific quality layers or regions on demand. This allows models to adapt in real-time, scaling input up or down based on confidence, available compute, or changes in the live feed. Subscription changes can occur in under 200 milliseconds.

## 7. Strategic Implications

The combination of VC-6 and swXtch.io changes the economics and scalability of live AI in several important ways.

## Operational efficiency

© 2025 Society of Motion Picture & Television Engineers® (SMPTE®)

A single multicast VC-6 stream can serve many AI tasks. The workflow eliminates redundant transcodes and separate transport paths. Models subscribe only to the data they need, which reduces bandwidth and lowers cloud egress charges. The approach also reduces intermediate storage for live clipping or partial replays.

## Scalability

Because the system is cloud native and built on multicast distribution, adding more AI workloads does not require additional encodes or new network routes. The same VC-6 stream can be fanned out to dozens of inference nodes with minimal additional load. This makes it possible to scale AI horizontally without creating bottlenecks in encoding or transport.

## Sustainability

Lower compute requirements for decoding and preprocessing mean reduced power consumption for both CPUs and GPUs. Bandwidth reductions also lower the energy footprint of transport. These efficiencies contribute to sustainability goals and can be measured in operational savings and reduced carbon impact.

## Standards alignment

VC-6 is a SMPTE standard and integrates cleanly with ST 2110 production environments. This ensures compatibility with existing broadcast and media systems, lowering the barrier to adoption and reducing integration risk. VC-6 can be deployed alongside existing tools and workflows without wholesale changes to production infrastructure.

## Technical implications

VC-6 with swXtch.io decouples the scale of AI inference from the constraints of source encoding and transport. The same core infrastructure can support new models, higher frame rates, or increased audience personalization without re-engineering the entire video path.

## 8. Conclusion

VC-6 and swXtch.io form a codec and network combination that is built for the way AI consumes live video. By integrating hierarchical, region-aware encoding in a multicast fabric, the system moves much of the preprocessing workload out of standalone servers and into the transport layer.

This shift reduces redundant compute, lowers bandwidth, and allows multiple AI workloads to operate in parallel from a single encoded source. Models can dynamically request the resolution or image regions they need, which makes the workflow adaptive and resource-aware.

The result is a path to scalable and efficient AI native live video processing that works within industry standards and can be deployed in cloud or hybrid environments. For teams that want to

expand AI in live production without driving up cost or complexity, VC-6 with swXtch.io provides a practical foundation.

- [2] SMPTE ST 2110: Professional Media Over Managed IP Networks.
- [3] V Nova internal benchmark data, 2025.
- [4] swXtch.io technical documentation, 2025.
- [5] NVIDIA Holoscan for Media developer documentation.

## Appendices

## Appendix A. Detailed benchmark tables and methodology

To be completed with benchmark tables and testing environment details.

## Appendix B. VC-6 MC transport protocol overview

VC-6 MC is an RTP over multicast transport designed to carry VC-6 bitstreams within the swXtch.io AI native network. It is based on RFC 3550 and uses a defined RTP payload type for VC-6, currently experimental.

## Key features and functions

- Packet structure: RTP header fields per RFC 3550 followed by VC-6 payload data. Sequence numbers and timestamps track frame order and timing.
- Multi LOQ support: Each packet can carry one or more levels of quality. Receivers can subscribe to specific levels to reduce bandwidth and decode load.
- ROI delivery: Packets can carry only the tiles or regions requested by a subscriber, enabling partial frame delivery in the transport layer.
- Multicast distribution: Streams are delivered using UDP multicast so multiple inference nodes can receive the same bitstream without duplicate transmission.

- Hybrid compatibility: Works alongside standard ST 2110 feeds in the same network, allowing production and AI to run in parallel.
- Integration points: Interoperates with the swXtch.io AI Gateway, Transcoder, and AI xNIC, as well as third party multicast receivers with VC-6 decode capability.
- Control layer: ROI and LOQ subscriptions can be managed dynamically through the MCP server so models can adjust requests in real time.

## Example packet layout

```
GLYPH<0> [ RTP Header | VC6 MC Payload Header | VC6 Payload Data ] VC6 MC Payload Header: - LOQ level (bits) - ROI coordinates (x, y, w, h) - Frame ID - Tile ID (if tiled transport is used)
```

GLYPH<0>

## Appendix C. Glossary

- AI xNIC : A network interface card implementation within the swXtch.io cloud architecture that can decode VC-6 or ST 2110 streams and deliver raw frames to applications.
- Intra frame codec : A video compression method that encodes each frame independently, enabling random access and low latency decoding.
- LOQ (level of quality) : A resolution layer in VC-6 that stores progressively more detail, allowing partial decoding at lower resolutions.
- MCP (Model Context Protocol) : A control protocol in the swXtch.io stack that allows AI models to monitor network state and request data dynamically.
- Multicast : A network transport method where a single stream is sent once and received by many endpoints simultaneously.
- ROI (region of interest) : A defined section of an image that can be decoded separately to reduce bandwidth and compute.

- SMPTE ST 2110 : A set of standards for professional media over IP networks used for live production.
- SMPTE ST 2117 1 (VC-6) : The SMPTE standard that defines the VC-6 codec, a hierarchical intra frame format optimized for scalable decoding and AI processing.
- Tokenization : The process of converting decoded image data into numerical embeddings for AI models.

**Brian Markwalter**

2025 is a year of change in the TV business.  Streaming is now consumers’ top choice for watching TV, by preferred video source, time spent viewing, and other common measures.  According to Pew Research Center, 83% of Americans watch streaming services, and for 55% of Americans streaming is their only source.  28% of Americans “double dip,” both subscribing to cable or satellite and watching streaming services.  Time spent viewing these sources followed suit. This year Nielsen reported, “Streaming reached a historic milestone in May as its share of total television usage outpaced the combined share of broadcast and cable for the first time ever.”

What about antenna usage? It is a distant third.  In Pew’s study, antenna users land in the “neither subscribe to cable or satellite nor watch streaming services” group, representing just 8% of consumers.  Another way to look at antenna usage is how many homes can access live TV via an antenna.  Horowitz Research says this figure declined from 32% in 2020 to 19% in 2025.  Nielsen’s public data is a little older, from January 2024, but matches Horowitz. Nielsen said that 22.75 million US households, or 18% of the 125 million TV households, access content through an antenna.

What has not changed is that Americans love their screens – and movies and TV shows. Televisions and smartphones are the top two technology products in U.S. consumers’ homes by a wide margin, with near-total penetration at 95% each. Laptops complete the screen trifecta with 73% ownership. According to CTA’s *The Video Ecosystem: The Future of TV report* , 85% of Americans reported watching movies and 82% reported watching TV shows in the past three months. News is third at 58%, and the combination of live sports, music videos, and long- and short-forum user generated content are all middle of the pack with about 50%.


The CTA Technology and Standards team has been busy working with industry to ensure consumers’ video entertainment experience gets better every year.  Here are some areas where our work made the biggest impact.

HDMI and CTA-861

Since its first publication in 2001, CTA-861 ( *A DTV Profile for Uncompressed High Speed Digital Interfaces* ) has played a critical role in the transition from analog to digital video interfaces on TVs and a wide range of other displays and video sources.  CTA-861 has a particularly symbiotic relationship with HDMI, underpinning audio and video signaling between sources and displays that use HDMI.  As A/V technology improves, CTA-861 needs regular updates to keep up with the needs of industry.  The standards committee that maintains CTA-861 has settled into a rhythm, producing a new baseline standard every two to three years.  Each major revision gets a new version letter following the standard number. The latest and greatest CTA-861 is revision J.  Changes in CTA-861-J include the following:

- Combined CTA-861-I with improvements contained in CTA-861.7
- Aligned Speaker Allocation Data Block (SADB) with industry requirements
- Added support for new features of VESA CVT in Video Timing Data Blocks (VTDBs)
- Clarified Data Blocks and InfoFrames, including defaultRGB, in the Colorimetry Data Block
- Deprecated DRA audio
- And as always, updated references

It’s not all about paperwork and PDFs.  CTA also hosts an annual CTA-861 Plugfest event.  CTA’s 861 Plugfest, typically held each October in California, brings manufacturers together to test interfaces, such as HDMI, HDCP and CEC, as part of a semi-private, round robin event.

The WAVE Project

The CTA WAVE Project (Web Application Video Ecosystem Project), which works to improve the global interoperability of internet-delivered commercial video, celebrated its 10 th anniversary in 2025. The WAVE Project references accepted industry standards like HTML5, MSE/EME, CENC, DASH, and HLS. As a key aspect of the project, participants maintain a complete, normative streaming player environment specification and interoperability tests to enable broad deployment of internet-delivered streaming media services. WAVE also enhances content delivery efficiencies and quality of service, with new protocols to exchange performance and route tracing data between clients and upstream sources such as Content Delivery Networks. The project also hosts the CMAF Industry Forum (CMAF-IF), which promotes CMAF industry interoperability and support.

WAVE has work underway on content preparation, web media API device support, device playback quality and validation, and standardized performance metadata exchanged between media clients and servers. Some specifications are paired with free open-source test programs and content to verify content and device performance. For example, the WAVE team has improved the device test suite released last year to make it easier to install and added new features, such as support for HEVC.

WAVE maintains key industry specifications, including the *Content Specification* (CTA-5001-F), an annual update to the *Web Media API Snapshot* (CTA-5000-H), *Device Playback Capabilities Specification* (CTA-5003-B), and *DASH-HLS Interoperability Specification* (CTA-5005-B). WAVE is also working on specifications to improve the flow of media to devices, including the *Common Media Client Data Specification* (CTA-5004-A), *Common Media Server Data* (CTA-5006), *Common Access Token Specification* (CTA-5007-B), and *Request Tracing Specification* (CTA-5008). WAVE also standardized the popular GeoHash specification as *Fast and Readable Geographical Hashing* (CTA-5009-A).

WAVE has also released an updated version of the *WAVE Streaming Media Test Suite for Devices* , a free open-source smart TV/media stick/set-top-box test suite for performance and compatibility verification of client platforms.

Energy Efficiency

Under two voluntary industry programs developed by CTA and NCTA, leading internet, cable, satellite, and telco service providers and equipment manufacturers continue to drive energy efficiency gains for set-top boxes, broadband modems, routers, and gateways. Leading TV manufacturers are making similar strides under a CTA-developed program.

Set-top box annual energy consumption fell by nearly three-quarters since 2012. A significant portion of this decline is due to subscriber reductions, but the weighted average power consumption of new set-top boxes also decreased by nearly two-thirds since 2013, even as functionality and features increased. This program uses ANSI/CTA-2043-B, Set-top Box (STB) Power Measurement.

Modems, routers and gateways all saw dramatic drops in the energy it takes to provide a gigabit of bandwidth to the consumer. Power per bit has been reduced by well over 80% and in some cases close to 90% since 2015. This program uses ANSI/CTA-2049-B, Determination of Small Network Equipment Average Energy Consumption, which will be incorporated into a new IEC standard (IEC 62087-8) to facilitate international harmonization.

Leading TV makers agreed to a standby power limit of 2 watts, a threshold that will go into effect in 2026. Negotiations toward an on-mode limit continue. The TV voluntary agreement is based on ANSI/CTA-2037-D, Determination of Television Set Power Consumption, now the U.S. Department of Energy test procedure for TVs. This agreement will also be incorporated into an IEC standard (IEC 62087-3) to facilitate international harmonization.

NEXTGEN TV


ATSC 3.0 is made possible by the transmission standards created by ATSC, but the toolbox of capabilities in ATSC 3.0 exceeds what any practical TV receiver can support. CTA fulfills a unique role in the ecosystem by producing the CTA-CEB32 suite of recommended practices for ATSC 3.0 TVs – closing the loop between transmission standards and receivers. CTA-CEB32 is a 10-part set of documents written for industry as guidance when designing ATSC 3.0 TVs.  CTA also developed the NEXTGEN TV logo program, so that consumers can easily identify ATSC 3.0 compatible TVs. Products bearing the NEXTGEN TV logo must pass an extensive suite of interoperability tests before going to market.  Every year the NEXTGEN TV test suite is updated to add tests as industry identifies new ATSC 3.0 features and interoperability concerns. The 2025 test suite now includes 475 tests and adds support for HDR10 playback and updated API schemas for interactivity support.

SMPTE Virtual Courses

Understanding SMPTE ST 2110

## Course Title: Understanding SMPTE ST 2110

Summary: 	This 6-module course provides learners with critical working knowledge of how SMPTE ST 2110 can be used to create professional media production or delivery systems which operate entirely within IP networks. This SMPTE virtual course will give learners both the knowledge and skills needed to help your facility take full advantage of ST 2110 and media over IP, which is an essential skill for any engineer or technologist working in today’s media and entertainment industry.

Description:	This virtual course begins with an overview of how media is managed within studio networks, followed by a discussion of why and how the ST 2110 standards suite was created, and highlights the advances from ST 2022-based IP media systems. The next portion of the course covers managing uncompressed video in live TV production, segmentation of a video image into sample row data for transport in RTP packets, and application of ST 2110 for bandwidth estimation. Audio and ancillary data are then addressed, including detailed explanations of interoperability with AES67 along with packetization and synchronization of captions and other metadata. The important topics of PTP timing and SDP media descriptions are the next topics covered. The course concludes with a look at how ST 2110 senders and receivers are required to control packet flows to ensure compatibility with IP network devices.

Course Outcomes:

Upon successful completion of this course, participants should be able to:

- Understand areas of application for both SMPTE ST 2110 and ST 2022
- Use SMPTE ST 2110-20 to calculate network signal bandwidths
- Discuss audio over IP, and particularly how SMPTE ST 2110-30 works with AES67 and other audio types
- List the ways that SMPTE ST 2110-40 governs ancillary data identification and packaging
- Describe both identification using IETF SDP and synchronization using IEEE 1588 PTP as specified in various SMPTE ST 2110 standards
- Explain traffic shaping and packet delivery timing, especially as indicated by SMPTE ST 2110-21

Module Topics:

- Module 1: Background and System Overview
- Module 2: Video Encapsulation
- Module 3: Audio Encapsulation
- Module 4: Data Encapsulation

## Leveraging Multi-Agent AI Systems for SMPTE ST 2110 Broadcast Automation

## TEJASWI MULAGADA, Technical Program Manager, M.S.CS

Alphacord Media Group, Centillion.AI

## Written for presentation & publication at the SMPTE 2025 Media and Technology Summit

Abstract . This paper proposes a multi-agent AI system to automate key tasks in SMPTE ST 2110 IP-based media workflows, focusing on real-time metadata tracking, dynamic queue buffering, and device configuration management. Orchestrated by a large language model (LLM), the system integrates specialized agents to improve efficiency, reduce errors, and ensure standards compliance, with human-in-the-loop safeguards for ethical alignment. Evaluations, conducted via network simulations using tools like ns-3 and Python-based emulators, demonstrate median latency reductions of 25-30% compared to FIFO baselines, false-positive rates of 2-5% for metadata anomaly detection, and recovery rates of 95-98% for configuration errors. These results are derived from synthetic datasets mimicking UHD video streams and benchmarked against traditional SNMP systems and modern reinforcement learning (RL) approaches. Developed as an original framework by the author, this system leverages collaborations for potential pilot testing and establishes a foundation for explainable AI in broadcast environments, with extensions to domains like live sports production.

Keywords . SMPTE ST 2110, multi-agent AI, broadcast automation, metadata tracking, queue buffer management, device configuration, large language model, IP media workflows, anomaly detection, NMOS interoperability.

## Introduction

The transition to IP-based media transport under the SMPTE ST 2110 standards suite has enabled scalable handling of uncompressed video, audio, and ancillary data, supporting high-bandwidth formats such as 4K and 8K. However, this shift introduces challenges in maintaining real-time synchronization, optimizing network performance, and ensuring device stability, particularly in dynamic live production settings. Issues like metadata desynchronization, buffer overflows during traffic spikes, and configuration drifts can lead to operational disruptions, as evidenced by industry reports on IP workflow inefficiencies.

Conventional approaches, including manual monitoring and Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)-based rules, are inadequate for the variability of IP environments. For instance, SNMP systems often react post-event, resulting in mean-time-to-repair (MTTR) delays of several minutes, per analyses from Cisco's IP multicast studies. This paper introduces a novel multi-agent AI framework to mitigate these bottlenecks, combining distributed agents with LLM orchestration and governance mechanisms. Drawing from emerging AI applications in media (e.g., SMPTE ER 1010:2023 on AI in production), the system aims to deliver quantifiable improvements in reliability and efficiency.

The contributions include: (1) a modular agent architecture tailored to ST 2110 specifics; (2) simulation-based evaluations with transparent methodologies; (3) governance frameworks for explainability and resilience; and (4) mappings to standards like NMOS IS-04/05 for practical integration. While preliminary results are simulation-derived, they align with realworld benchmarks from Intel and Cisco, setting the stage for field validations through partnerships.

## Proposed Multi-Agent AI System

The framework comprises three specialized agents, coordinated by an LLM (e.g., based on models like GPT-4 or Llama), which analyzes contextual inputs and delegates tasks. Integration occurs via APIs compatible with AMWA NMOS for device discovery and control, ensuring interoperability in ST 2110 ecosystems.

## Metadata Tracking Agent

This agent processes ancillary data streams (e.g., per ST 2110-40) using machine learning models such as isolation forests or autoencoders for real-time anomaly detection. It categorizes content (e.g., subtitles, timing signals) and flags issues like packet malformations. Implementation draws from frameworks in Khan et al. (2024), where metadata anomaly detection in key-management systems achieved 2-4% false-positive rates on datasets of 10,000+ samples.

## Queue Buffer Agent

Employing predictive analytics (e.g., via LSTM networks in TensorFlow), this agent dynamically adjusts switch buffers to handle variable loads in high-format transmissions (ST 2110-20/30). It predicts spikes based on traffic patterns, reducing latency as seen in Cisco's buffer optimization reports (20-40% gains in multicast IP).

## Configuration Agent

This monitors' network devices using graph-based algorithms (e.g., NetworkX for topology mapping), detecting misconfigurations via NMOS IS-04 queries. It proposes corrections, escalating to humans for approval, with recovery inspired by self-healing systems in SuperAGI (2024), reporting 95-99% efficacy in automated repairs.

The LLM orchestrator parses inputs (e.g., "High latency detected in stream X") and generates explanations, e.g., "Delegating to Queue Agent due to predicted 50ms spike per ST 2110-30 timing constraints." Human-in-the-loop is enforced at decision points, complying with EU AI Act high-risk classifications.


Figure 1. Multi-Agent System Architecture: A flowchart illustrating LLM orchestration, with arrows showing task delegation from the LLM to the three agents (Metadata Tracking, Queue Buffer, Configuration), feedback loops for human oversight, and integration with ST 2110 streams.


## Evaluation Framework

To ensure rigor, evaluations emphasize methodological transparency, addressing feedback on simulation details and baselines.

Test Bed Setup : Simulations were conducted using ns-3 (version 3.38), a discrete-event network simulator, configured to emulate ST 2110 environments. Virtual nodes represented switches, senders, and receivers with PTP (Precision Time Protocol) synchronization. Traffic models included synthetic UHD video streams (e.g., 10-100 Gbps bursts), generated via FFmpeg tools to mimic real IP packets. Datasets: 5,000-10,000 samples per agent, sourced from public repositories like GitHub's media-packet datasets or synthesized with random variations (e.g., 5-10% noise for anomalies).

## Micro-Benchmarks

Queue Buffer Agent: Tested on variable loads (e.g., 40 Gbps studio scale), measuring latency via packet timestamps. Adaptive buffering reduced median delays from 50ms (FIFO) to 35ms, a 30% gain, consistent with Intel's FPGA-NIC benchmarks (2022).

Metadata Tracking Agent: Evaluated on injected anomalies (e.g., malformed SDP files), using scikit-learn models trained on 80/20 split datasets. False-positive rates: 2-5%, outperforming traditional rule-based detection (18% per comparative studies).

Configuration Agent: Injected errors (e.g., mismatched NMOS registries) across 100 trials; recovery via automated fixes achieved 95-98%, versus manual baselines (85%).

import numpy as np from scipy.stats import norm # Simulate traffic: normal dist for packet arrivals arrivals = np.cumsum(norm.rvs(loc=10, scale=2, size=1000))  # ms intervals buffer_size = 50  # initial latencies = [] for i in range(1, len(arrivals)): delay = max(0, arrivals[i] - arrivals[i-1] - buffer_size) latencies.append(delay) # Adaptive adjust: increase buffer if delay > threshold if delay > 20: buffer_size += 10 median_latency = np.median(latencies)  # Example: ~35ms vs 50ms baseline

This yields verifiable results; full scripts in Appendix A.

## Scalability Tests

Assessed across scales-OB van (10 Gbps, <2 GB RAM), studio (40 Gbps, 3-4 GB), backbone (100 Gbps, 5 GB). Reconfiguration latency: <1s, with CPU utilization under 20% on standard hardware.

## Comparative Experiments : Benchmarked against:

- SNMP rules: 40% higher MTTR (e.g., 120s vs. 72s).
- Single-agent RL (Q-learning baselines from networking papers): 15-20% inferior in anomaly handling.
- Hybrid monitoring (e.g., from SuperAGI): Multi-agent showed 10% better recovery.

Metrics: MTTR, missed alarms (<1%), operator interactions (reduced 50%).

## About Tables

## Governance, Explainability, and Resilience

## Responsibility Matrix

| Scenario            | Operator Role        | Vendor Role           | AI Role                          | Mitigation Strategy                                              |
|---------------------|----------------------|-----------------------|----------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Metadata Anomaly    | Approve corrections  | Device testing        | Detect (2-5% FP)                 | Human veto; fallback to manual sync; integrate with NMOS logging |
| Buffer Overflow     | Crisis intervention  | Hardware optimization | Adjust (25-30% reduction)        | LLM rerouting; audit trails via Syslog                           |
| Configuration Error | Change authorization | Firmware updates      | Propose fixes (95- 98% recovery) | Audit logging; cross-check with PTP masters                      |

## **Explainability**

LLM rationales are validated through ensemble methods-e.g., comparing outputs to rulebased verifiers (e.g., via LangChain tools) to mitigate hallucinations, achieving 90% accuracy in reasoning benchmarks from OpenAI guides. Rationales integrate into existing workflows by exporting to ELK Stack logs, aligning with IEEE Ethically Aligned Design.

## **Resilience**

Fallbacks switch to SNMP on LLM downtime; adversarial inputs are filtered via robustness checks (e.g., ART toolbox). Red teaming simulates edge cases, like high-noise streams.

## **Results**

Simulations validate claims: Queue buffering: 25-30% latency drops (graphs in Figure 2). Metadata: 2-5% FPs. Configuration: 95-98% recovery. Multi-agent outperforms baselines by 40% in MTTR, with low overhead.

Figure 2. Performance Graphs: Line charts depicting latency reduction over time, false-positive rate distributions, and recovery accuracy percentages.


## Strategic Partnership

Core ideas are author's original; partnerships with Alphacord and Centillion enable pilots. Future: XAI dashboard (NASA-TLX validated); annexes to ST 2110-30/EBU R-148; ethics via red teaming; extensions to ST 2038/IMF/OTT.

## Future Work

XAI Dashboard : Real-time visualization of agent flows and confidence scores, validated via NASA-TLX for reduced cognitive load (20-30%).

Standard Mappings : Annex proposals linking agents to ST 2110-30 (timing), EBU R-148 (NMOS), and JT-NM TR-1001-1 (interoperability).

Ethics Simulations : Red teaming for edge cases, balancing efficiency and editorial responsibility.

Cross-Domain Extensions : Adaptations for ST 2038 live sports metadata, IMF quality control, and OTT ad-insertion.

## Conclusion

This multi-agent AI system transforms ST 2110 workflows by automating bottlenecks with proven efficiency gains. Its explainable, resilient design-rooted in the author's visionpaves the way for industry-wide adoption, enhancing broadcast reliability amid IP transitions.

This framework advances ST 2110 automation with evidence-backed efficiency, setting benchmarks for AI in broadcasting.

## Acknowledgements

This work represents the author's independent research and original ideas. Gratitude to Alphacord Media Group for summit representation and to Centillion AI for potential pilot support.

Appendix A: Sample Codes This appendix provides the full Python scripts used for simulations in the evaluation framework, as referenced in the Micro-Benchmarks section. These are verifiable and based on libraries like NumPy and SciPy for traffic modeling and latency calculations.

## Queue Buffer Simulation Script:

import numpy as np from scipy.stats import norm # Simulate traffic arrivals with normal distribution (mean 10ms interval, std 2ms) arrivals = np.cumsum(norm.rvs(loc=10, scale=2, size=1000))  # Cumulative arrivals in ms # Initial buffer size buffer_size = 50  # ms # List to store latencies latencies = [] # Calculate delays and adaptively adjust buffer for i in range(1, len(arrivals)): inter_arrival = arrivals[i] - arrivals[i-1] delay = max(0, inter_arrival - buffer_size) latencies.append(delay) # Adaptive adjustment: Increase buffer if delay exceeds threshold if delay > 20: buffer_size += 10 # Compute median latency median_latency = np.median(latencies) print(f"Median Latency: {median_latency:.2f} ms")  # Example output: ~35ms vs. 50ms baseline

## Metadata Anomaly Detection Example (using scikit-learn Isolation Forest):

from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest import numpy as np # Synthetic metadata samples (e.g., packet sizes, timestamps; 5000 samples, 2 features) data = np.random.normal(loc=100, scale=10, size=(5000, 2)) # Inject anomalies (5% noise) anomalies = np.random.normal(loc=200, scale=50, size=(250, 2)) data = np.vstack([data[:4750], anomalies]) # Train Isolation Forest model (80/20 split implied in full eval) model = IsolationForest(contamination=0.05, random_state=42) model.fit(data) # Predict anomalies (-1 for anomaly, 1 for normal) predictions = model.predict(data) # Calculate false-positive rate (assuming ground truth labels: last 250 are anomalies) labels = np.array([1] * 4750 + [-1] * 250) fp_rate = np.sum((predictions == -1) & (labels == 1)) / len(labels) * 100 print(f"False-Positive Rate: {fp_rate:.2f}%")  # Example: 2-5%

## AI-Assisted Post-Production: Enhancing Workflows with AI Interpolation and Object Detection

Brian Gaffney, MTI FILM

## Written for presentation at the SMPTE 2025 Media and Technology Summit

## Abstract

AI-assisted methods are redefining workflows in post-production, enabling faster turnaround and more precise automation without sacrificing creative control. Recent advances in deep learning have produced practical solutions for long-standing technical challenges such as frame rate conversion, slate detection for dailies, and restoration of missing or damaged frames.

This paper presents technical details of three such applications: (1) the use of RIFE interpolation augmented by NVIDIA TensorRT for accurate AI-based frame rate conversion, (2) object detection using Ultralytics YOLOv11 for slate identification in dailies workflows, and (3) generative AI -based frame inference for restoration of archival film. Case studies -including the recent 4K restoration of Sunset Boulevard at USC -illustrate how targeted models trained on relevant datasets can accelerate creative processes in production and restoration while keeping human operators firmly in control.

## 1. Introduction

The convergence of artificial intelligence and traditional post-production has introduced new efficiencies to creative workflows. Beyond generative models for scene synthesis and storytelling, task-specific AI systems are now addressing long-standing bottlenecks in the technical domain. Video frame interpolation, intelligent object detection, and generative frame

reconstruction are three areas where measurable improvements are already being seen in production and restoration environments.

Rather than replacing human operators, these AI models function as assistive systems: automating tedious or repetitive tasks, reducing error-prone manual labor, and allowing artists and technicians to spend more time on higher-value quality control and creative decisionmaking.

This paper discusses three cornerstone technologies:

- AI-based frame rate conversion -powered by RIFE (Real-Time Intermediate Flow Estimation) and accelerated by NVIDIA TensorRT, enabling precise interpolation between frames for professional mastering and international delivery.
- AI object-based slate detection -fine-tuned Ultralytics YOLOv11 models trained to identify the 'slate clap' moment across dailies rolls, reducing manual search times.
- Generative AI frame inference for restoration -temporal and learned models that reconstruct missing or severely damaged frames in archival or degraded material.

## Examples from Submarine., Topkapi, and Designing Woman.

illustrate their application and reliability. These techniques demonstrate a new collaborative relationship between human artistry and machine intelligence in post-production.

## 2. AI Frame Interpolation with RIFE and TensorRT

Traditional optical flow interpolation is computationally expensive and often introduces artifacts, especially in scenes with fast lateral motion, occlusions, or complex lighting. RIFE, a deeplearning-based method for frame interpolation, uses dynamic attention mechanisms to estimate motion and synthesize intermediate frames with remarkable temporal coherence.

The challenge is to synthesize new frames but respect the time base, motion within a scene, light, reflections and all detail within the surrounding frames without generating undo artifacting.

At MTI FILM, we have integrated RIFE into our pipeline and optimized its inference time using NVIDIA's TensorRT runtime. TensorRT accelerates the execution of trained models on NVIDIA GPUs by converting PyTorch-based networks into a high-performance runtime format. Through precision calibration (FP16/INT8) and kernel fusion, we achieved real-time or faster-than-realtime frame interpolation for common frame rate conversions, such as:

- 23.976fps to 25fps for international delivery
- 29.97fps to 23.976fps for cinematic repurposing and UHD remastering

This solution powers the AI-based frame rate conversion , offering frame synthesis accuracy sufficient for professional-grade deliverables. The tool has been especially useful in restoring legacy broadcast material or preparing international masters without introducing cadence errors or ghosting.

## a. What is Video Frame Interpolation (VFI)?

VFI is the process of creating new frames to insert between existing ones in a video, effectively increasing the video's frame rate. This leads to smoother, more fluid motion, especially noticeable in slow-motion or fast-action sequences that exhibit high contrast, typical of digital cameras capturing at 23.98fps.

## b. How RIFE Works:

RIFE utilizes a neural network called IFNet to estimate the intermediate flow (motion) between frames. It then uses this flow information to synthesize new frames, essentially predicting where pixels should move from one frame to the next.

Unlike some other methods, RIFE doesn't rely on pre-trained optical flow models and can handle arbitrary time-step interpolation. MTI FILM integrated this model into an editing platform CORTEX, to allow all of the supported restoration file formats such as DPX, EXR, TIFF as well as ProRes and all camera supported codecs to be frame converted. This was the larger challenge, getting these tools to understand timecode and frame count and to maintain consistency across the time base of the source media.

This tool was designed to also work with IMF creations and supports DOLBY Vision 5.0 so that converted files can ingest the source XML containing the DOLBY Vision metadata and the synthesized media will create unique JSON files per clip that are concatenated into one file and reprocessed via DOLBY Metafier. This newly generated XML contains the updated frame converted cut points that match the new cut points. QC of the transforms proves the process works properly. This use case of AI assisted artists with MTai FrameConvert has been used successfully on major A-Title films since 2022.

## Conversion Result Examples

## 3. Automated Slate Detection Using YOLOv11

One of the most time-consuming manual tasks for a dailies operator is identifying the precise frame when the film slate closes -critical for sound synchronization. One approach to address this is to use AI based Object Detection for model training . Using the finetuned Ultralytics'

YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once, version 11) object detection model using and a proprietary dataset of over 10,000 manually annotated frames containing slates in various positions and lighting conditions from various television productions and archives.

## The model detects:

- Slate presence
- Open vs. closed state
- Timecode metadata is detected using the Audio waveform metadata
- (No OCR is currently used) due to issues related to production

By integrating this into the AI based Object Detection module, the system searches for and tries to flag the exact "clap" frame across camera rolls, reducing manual search time from minutes to seconds with object detection.

Object detection is a task that involves identifying the location and class of objects in an image or video stream. The output of an object detector is a set of bounding boxes that enclose the objects in the image, along with class labels and confidence scores for each box. Object detection is a good choice when you need to identify objects of interest in a scene, but don't need to know exactly where the object is or its exact shape.


This AI-assisted solution is particularly beneficial in multi-cam environments or when metadata is incomplete or inconsistent. The tool enables operators to spend more time reviewing sync

quality instead of hunting for the correct frame of a closed slate. Frame accuracy is dependent on visibility as slates may not even appear in a frame during Wild Track or repeated takes.

The image below shows the flagged frame that the MTai SlateDetect, using the Yolov11 model, was trained on. Several training passes using well over 10,00 frames that were manually annotated as Open, Closed, or No-Slate so that the system could train and learn and produce a model that has been incorporated into commercial products for dailies. The system detects in milliseconds the slates and displays these detected marked slates as ORANGE for 'found slate' and GREEN for 'found closed slate' and RED 'found no slate' and this status assist the dailies operators QC process and allows them to vet the detection and confirm to auto-sync sound and picture of offset and accept to refine the AI detection. This process reduces the search and seek method of manual dailies and allows operators to further inspect the notes, comments, adjust for off-speed materials and any custom camera formats introduced as is often in a new show supporting dailies. Example Video

## 4. Restoration with Generative AI Frame Inference

Generative AI frame inference combines temporal modeling with edge-aware optical flow to reconstruct missing or unrepairable frames. This has proven invaluable in reviving archival footage where traditional manual or optical techniques are insufficient.

In collaboration with Paramount Pictures, this technique was used in the 2024 4K restoration of Sunset Boulevard . According to Charlotte Barker, Director of Restoration Services at Paramount, the process restored 14 instances of missing frames and jump cuts, while maintaining consistency in grain structure and character detail.

The system leverages GAN-refined synthesis steps to ensure results that are visually indistinguishable from neighboring frames during playback and grading. This technique extends beyond missing material to frames with extreme warping, water damage, raking, or other irreparable physical defects.

## 5. Results and Discussion

All three three of the listed AI cornerstone technologies share a design philosophy: AI should serve artists by reducing tedium, not replacing judgment. Key results include:

| Technology                      | Avg. Time Saved      | Accuracy        | Use Case                 |
|---------------------------------|----------------------|-----------------|--------------------------|
| AI-based Frame Rate Conversion  | 10x vs. optical flow | <1% frame error | 23.976 - 25fps mastering |
| AI Object-Based Slate Detection | 2 - 4 sec/clip       | >98% detection  | Sound sync for dailies   |

| GenAI Frame Inference for   | N/A (restoration)   | Artist-   | Missing/damaged   |
|-----------------------------|---------------------|-----------|-------------------|

## 6. Limitations and Quality Control

All content to be frame converted requires frame breaks or an EDL to let the RIFE interpolation model know that a new source should be loaded and interpolated and that the frame before was not contiguous to the new scene. These unmarked events can cause unwanted "hallucinations" with the interpolation. This occurs primarily on:

- Lateral Motion on a scene break
- When Source detail is only existing for one frame
- Tends to occur on breaks at the beginning and end of scenes

Various applications can perform automatic shot detection but ideally an EDL or XML file are provided to provide an exact reference.

QC is required and when a hallucination is generated, the system provides the ability to playback both frame rates simultaneously, in sync, and allows for full frame replacement from the source or the ability to paint within a frame to correct any aberrations.

Providing an ability to correct the AI assist is critical and another example of why AI tools won't replace artists but rather assist them in providing a better restored product. See below, a 23.98 and 29.97 source can be viewed and played in sync and frames painted or replaced with a simple shift-insert command or in frame painting process.


The frame on the right shows distortion caused by AI Interpolation on lateral movement. Especially when breaking frame and entering from off axis can cause a frame or two of distortion that needs to be replaced using AI restoration tools such as Paint and Frame replacement techniques

## 7. Conclusion and Future Work

AI is proving its value across post-production tasks -when trained and deployed correctly. In practice, AI-assisted artistry enables operators to remain in creative control while reducing technical burdens.

Future development will focus on:

- Expanding generative frame inference for noise reduction and flicker correction
- Enhancing object detection for QC tasks (e.g., boom mics, crew reflections, signage)
- Investigating diffusion-based inpainting for gate hair and fine-grain restoration

AI will not replace artists -but it will redefine their workflows, providing an assistive layer that extends human capability.

## Why does a shutter mode LED 3D display give serious fatigue to the audience?

1. In shutter-mode systems, many neural cells involved in short-term memory must work intensively to store alternating images. This is why in a shutter mode system, the 'fatigue' produced.
2. Fast 2D or 3D movement of objects within a 3D video can cause distortion or a reduction in 3D resolution.
- a)  Polarizing display with one-D movement object
- b)  shutter display  with one-D movement object
- c)  Polarizing display with two-D movement object
- d) shutter display with two-D movement object, the black should be at left forever but now the L7 is at left of R8 then both time and space errors occurred.


So, in a shutter mode system, the 3D distortion occurred, or say 3D resolution decreased.

## LED 3D Cinema Display -- the future display system in cinemas

## Written for presentation at the

## SMPTE 2025 Media and Technology Summit

Abstract . This paper presents a novel approach to 3D cinema display using LED technology, with particular emphasis on mitigating 3D-induced visual discomfort, commonly referred to as "3D Vertigo Syndrome." For over a century, since Gabriel Lippmann proposed the principle of micro-mirror matrix stereoscopic display, the vision for advanced displays has consistently included both high-definition (HD) resolution and immersive three-dimensional (3D) experiences. Among the various 3D display systems developed, stereoscopic cinema remains the most widely adopted by the public. Even in the foreseeable future, the situation is expected to remain the same. However, traditional projection-based 3D systems often suffer from limitations such as image crosstalk and viewer discomfort, which continue to hinder widespread acceptance and long-term audience engagement.

This paper introduces a direct-view LED-based 3D cinema display system designed to significantly reduce image crosstalk and improve viewer comfort. Unlike projector-based systems that depend on screen reflectivity and viewing geometry, LED panels offer higher brightness, better contrast, and pixellevel  control,  enabling  more  precise  image  separation  for  stereoscopic  content.  Experimental observations indicate that the proposed system exhibits minimal crosstalk between left and right eye images, a key factor contributing to visual fatigue and discomfort in traditional 3D environments.

A primary focus of this study is to eliminate 3D vertigo syndrome, a condition characterized by nausea, dizziness, and disorientation. Some viewers may experience this symptom after prolonged viewing of 3D content. A series of long-term audience tests has shown that, compared to the traditional projectionbased system, these symptoms do not appear when using the proposed polarized LED 3D display system, and the so-called 3D fatigue is significantly reduced.

Here, the paper describes a polarizing mode LED 3D cinema display, and the practical viewing result is quite different from that of some regular LED 2D screens that use the shutter mode by adding a frame frequency doubler to play a 3D movie.

Keywords. LED 3D Displays, 3D vertigo syndrome, Polarizing, DCHD, ROCOS.

## 1. Research and development on overcoming 3D vertigo syndrome

According to records, the world's first 3D movie was The Power of Love , but unfortunately, this is only a record; the Bwana Devil is the first color 3D feature movie. The Magician's Adventures is the first color widescreen stereoscopic film in China, and it was produced in 1962. Since then, the topic of dizziness after watching 3D movies has gained attention in China, even though it was not a serious issue before the release of the famous 3D movie Avatar.

In 1988 and 1990, a series of giant outdoor video screens was created for the 11th Asian Olympic Games in Beijing. Since 1990, special R&D efforts have been underway. Initially, the goal was to find an optimal display method for stereoscopic movies that would not have a negative impact on personal health. Then, after 7 years of R&D, the first shut-down mode LED video 3D screen was developed in 1997, which was essentially a standard 2D screen with the addition of a frame frequency doubler. When it was transported to Los Angeles, it was accepted by neither Disneyland nor Hollywood. To improve the performance of 3D displays, further R&D efforts for polarizing LED 3D displays were initiated. In 2009, the film Avatar , a famous 3D movie, was produced. Then, in 2011, the first Interlacing polarizing LED 3D display and the first DCHD (Dual Channel High Definition) polarizing LED 3D display were produced. Then, another DCHD (Dual Channel High Definition) polarizing LED 3D display was produced.

Previously, almost all papers and reports had pointed out that any 3D movie inevitably produces 3D dizziness or other adverse effects. Numerous tests and reports can support this conclusion. However, all reports intentionally overlook the fact that people's eyes are also dual cameras, which can send images from both the left and right eyes to the central nervous system, generating 3D sensations. Why doesn't dizziness or vertigo occur when people see any object in 3D in their daily lives? Another fact is that, over a long time, the correctness of the so-called 20 millisecond persistence phenomenon of the human eye has been questioned in R&D. Since the start of R&D aimed at developing a heathy 3D display, it had been noticed that any conclusions must be consistent with the basic principle that the human eyes are merely two sensors, while the central nervous system acts as the processor, ultimately determining what is perceived. The basic idea from the very beginning is to enable the central nervous system to make accurate decisions about what is seen.

From the beginning, we read all relevant reports and papers and attempted to use the testing method used by Professor Solimini [2]. In the abstract of his paper, it is described as: ' The increasing popularity of  commercial movies showing three-dimensional (3D) images have raised concern about possible adverse side effects on viewers. Methods and Findings: A prospective, carryover observational study was designed to assess the effect of exposure (3D vs. 2D movie views) on self-reported symptoms of visually induced motion sickness. The standardized Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) was selfadministered on a convenience sample of 497 healthy adult volunteers before and after viewing 2D and 3D movies. Viewers reporting some sickness (SSQ total score, 15) comprised 54.8% of the total sample after the 3D movie, compared to 14.1% of the total sample after the 2D movie. Symptom intensity was 8.8 times higher than the baseline after exposure to a 3D movie (compared to the increase of 2 times the baseline after the 2D movie). Multivariate modeling of visually induced motion sickness, as a response variable, highlighted the significant effects of exposure to 3D movies, a history of car sickness and headache, after adjusting for gender, age, self-reported anxiety level, attention to the movie,  and  showtime.  Conclusions:  Viewing  3D  movies  can  exacerbate  symptoms  of  nausea, oculomotor disturbances, and disorientation, especially in women with a susceptible visual-vestibular system. Confirmatory studies, which include examination of clinical signs on viewers, are needed to pursue  conclusive  evidence  on  the  3D  vision  effects  on  spectators.
