From all the tests and experiments, it is clear that 3D vertigo occurs only when two eyes perceive different images, rather than two views of the same scene, as in normal vision. Any factor, such as optical jitter or other forms of asynchrony, that prevents the central nervous system from correctly fusing the images can trigger '3D Vertigo Syndrome.'

A study conducted with a sample size of at least 5,000 individuals focused on the primary issue of viewing 3D video. The findings were then compared to the results obtained from a projector system evaluated by Prof. Solimini.

A series of tests confirmed that the polarized "LED 3D cinema display" system does not cause "3D vertigo syndrome." When testing the four screen layouts mentioned earlier, all b), c), and d) did not receive any reports of discomfort. However, for a large project, the tests and questionnaires mainly focus on two setups: a) two screens in the workshop and b) another fixed installation location site. Even for these two places, the feedback of 3D vertigo is almost zero at the beginning. When conducting tests, any discomfort should not be overlooked or missed. Each time for the test, the audience was asked to watch two or three 3D movies for at least five hours at a time. Then, a series of surveys was conducted among all those who had viewed polarizing 3D LED movies. According to reports, final statistics, and summaries,  the  number  is  5.8%.  However,  viewers  who  feel  unwell  may  experience  any  of  the symptoms listed below. It should be noted that this does not constitute "3D vertigo." In fact, such a test cannot be considered a fair comparison to projector-based tests, because the conditions employed here are significantly more stringent than those used when viewing 3D films on a projector. Notably, even individuals who spend five hours in front of a computer screen without exposure to any 3D content may still experience discomfort.

- a. Individuals who feel vertigo even when they watch a normal 2D movie.

b. In daily life, individuals who will feel vertigo when they see somebody performing strenuous exercise, e.g., brandishing a knife or a sword?

- c. Individuals who will feel unwell when riding a bus or a boat.
- d. Individuals who have never worn any glasses.
- e.  Individuals  thinking  that  there  must  be  vertigo  on  3D  -  even  before  they  experienced  it. (psychological suggestion)

Based on the tests, individuals in d and e above could show improvement over time, whereas some others may never be suitable. However, during the entire testing process, there were no extremely severe cases, such as vomiting. Here, it is worth noting that the 5.8% figure includes some participants who were already unwell before the test. For instance, some individuals became ill after drinking at noon, but still participated in the test without telling us in advance.

## Configurations of Practical Polarizing LED 3D Displays

A series of polarizing LED 3D displays was developed.

First, DCHD (Dual Channel High Definition) Mode Polarizing 3D Display. This is illustrated in Fig. 1.15, and it represents the perfect or full Polarizing 3D.

Fig. 1.15 LED pixel Configuration for DCHD           Fig. 1.16 LED pixel configuration for Interlacing (Fig. 2 in patent number US 10,298,919 B2)            (Fig. 6 in patent number US 10,298,919 B2)



In the Fig. 1.15 configuration, each physical pixel consists of two individual pixels, one for the left and one for the right. With this configuration, the display can play full movie pixels without any loss. It is clear that the cost is higher.

To reduce the costs, the basic configuration of an interlacing system is similar to that of a standard 2D LED screen (Fig. 1.16). When polarizing film is applied to the LED boards, the configuration changes accordingly. During 3D playback, the vertical resolution is divided, with half of the pixels assigned to the left and the other half to the right. For this configuration, a series of tests were conducted in multiple experiments, and it was found that the viewing result is still significantly better than that of any projector or a shutter mode LED display, and it outperforms a standard projector system. As this configuration of displays suffers from vertical resolution loss, even if the practical result is still significantly better than either a shutter mode LED system or a projector system, to avoid any possible misunderstanding, it should be clearly labeled as an Interlacing Polarizing 3D display.

However, from the very primary TV theories, it is known that the vertical resolution of the human eye is lower than the horizontal resolution. Throughout the entire test and experiment procedure, for both configuration modes, the audience did not notice a particularly significant difference between the two.

## Main specs of the polarizing film

As the temperature of the LED display surface can reach up to 40°C-50 °C, the polarizing film must be able to work continuously; therefore, it is very necessary to undergo the Reliability test as outlined in the table. Specifically, it must pass the high-temperature test at 95 ℃ (203°F) for 600 hours, and the change must be less than 3%. Provided that the test characteristics of high temperature, high humidity, and other reliability indicators are not lower than those shown in the table. If not, once the polarizing film cannot function at such a temperature, its polarizing function will decrease gradually over time, a process known as depolarization. Once that occurs, the direct issue is that the crosstalk becomes higher. However, if production quality is well-controlled, such an issue won't occur. One screen was produced in 2014 and began testing that same year; it is still under testing at the time of writing. By using the general calculation formula: Crosstalk ratio = [(brightness value of left-eye image in right-eye display area + brightness value of right-eye image in left - eye display area) divided by (brightness value of left - eye image in left-eye display area + brightness value of right-eye image in right-eye display area) x100%, to test, the crosstalk is still no higher than 1.3%, and this is much better than a projector crosstalk that could be more than 10%, even 20% [8].

## Critical and very special tests and experiments

Using the method of reduction to absurdity to prove certain situations in R&D is also a commonly employed approach. Since none of the polarizing screens produced 3D vertigo, we began to consider how to enable a screen to produce 3D vertigo by modifying something or altering the application process. A series of special tests and experiments was used here.

1. First, it was believed that 3D vertigo occurs when certain factors cause the two eyes to perceive different things, making it difficult for the central nervous system to interpret what is happening. Typically, the two eyes should perceive the same object from two different sides. However, when they perceive two entirely different things instead of two sides of a single object, 3D vertigo can occur. Based on this reasoning, a delay line with 200-meter super category 5 or 6 cables has been inserted between the dual transmission lines. Its transmission rate is 1000 Mbps, and its delay time is  approximately  500  ns/100  m  at  250  MHz.  Therefore,  the  200-meter  cable's  delay  time  is approximately  one  microsecond.  Then,  the  delay  line  was  reduced  to  500  ns.  Among  the participants being tested, some felt better, but others still did not feel well. Then, the delay line was

increased to 2 microseconds. All the people under test felt unwell, although the intensity of their symptoms varied. This finding is similar to those of Professor Solimini. Whenever the tests were administered, not all participants experienced precisely the same sensations. Additionally, when we attempted to change the cables from different manufacturers, the test situation also revealed some differences.

Fig. 1.17 Of the dual transmission lines, one had a delay line inserted for testing.


Fig.  1.18  conducts  a  very  special  test  using  two  cameras,  but  in  different  directions.  Further experiments and tests were conducted. Similarly, two different video players were used to play different videos. In either case, severe Vertigo occurred, which was far more intense than that experienced when watching 3D movies on a projector-based system. All participants in the test reported immediate nausea and an urge to vomit after only a few seconds of viewing.


These  experiments  and  test  results  appear  to  support  the  original  hypothesis.  That  is,  the synchronization provided by a projector-based system is insufficient. Several factors may contribute to this situation, including, but not limited to, optical jitter caused by temperature or power fluctuations, as well as transmission-related issues. For example, in a projector movie player system, the dual projectors can appear to be using just one synchronization input. However, from the input (1) to the final display DMD micro mirror (4), it has to pass the transmission (2) and (3) processing procedures. After the input, there is no possibility of any genlock between two (2), three (3), and four (4), especially

at the (4), where there are mechanical actions, and possible differences due to temperature and power factors.  Specifically,  there  is  no  synchronization  between  any  two  pixels  on  the  DMDs  of  the  two machines. Even slight differences can cause the central nervous system to perceive a 3D vertigo effect. In a DCHD 3D LED video player, the two pixels for both left and right pictures can be controlled by a single power line, a feature known as absolute sync. These are quite different, as there are many kinds and types of projectors. It is challenging to obtain precise data for all. However, this series of tests suggests that differences of just a few nanoseconds could induce 3D vertigo in the audience. This varies from person to person and situation to situation. Similar to being on a cruise ship during sudden strong winds, some individuals in good health may experience severe seasickness, while others with only average physical fitness remain unaffected.

. 1.21 The big difference in driving between a projector and an LED screen


What accounts for the significant  variation  in  vertigo  experienced  across  different  programs?  One phenomenon is that when the 3D Ratio of an Object Coming Out of the Screen (ROCOS) becomes larger, the 3D vertigo syndrome worsens. Is this why, so far, most 3D movies have not made much more progress with bigger screens? It should be noted that when a cinema uses such a polarizing 3D LED display, the movie director no longer needs to worry about the size of the ROCOS, and it can be just  as  the  director  originally  intended.  This  is  simply  a  manifestation  of  the  3D  vertigo  syndrome, reflecting a limitation of the directors' original approach. Here, the conclusion is very encouraging! In a polarized 3D LED cinema display system, 3D vertigo syndrome will not occur-regardless of the size of the ROCOS-provided that left and right image signals are perfectly synchronized. This precise synchronization is a key advantage that all 3D movie directors are likely to value.

## 2.  Why in a polarizing 3D LED system, the crosstalk is so small

This principle is much simpler.

A. In an LED system, issues such as defocus, misconvergence, reflection, glare, and speckle, which can occur in laser projector systems, are absent.

B. During screen production, the selection of materials and quality control must be precise.  As a result, the crosstalk in a polarized 3D LED system is significantly lower than that in a projector-based system.

The above are the main reasons why, in a polarizing LED 3D system, crosstalk is significantly reduced. Practically, by the test, the separation of both left and right images in a projector system can be as low as 95% or even lower. But it is no less than 99% in a polarizing 3D LED system. According to practical tests, the efficiency can reach up to 99.8% when the screen has just been produced. Therefore, the crosstalk should be approximately 0.2% initially, and may increase to a maximum of 2% after a period of operation. This is quite different from the 5% or even higher rate of a projector system. One report [8] even indicates that the crosstalk of a projector can be as high as 10-20%.

## 3. Problems of Shutting Mode LED 3D Screen

Work began in 1990, and in 1997, after seven years of research and development, the world's first shutter mode 3D LED video display was created. From the very beginning, the goal was to find the best way to play a stereoscopic movie, enabling the audience to have a significantly enhanced visual experience compared to existing projection systems. During the long-term R&D process, numerous discoveries were made, ranging from shutter-mode to polarizing-mode 3D LED screens. As R&D on large, viewer-friendly 3D displays continued, it was found that shutter-mode 3D LED displays have serious  shortcomings  beyond  the  numerous  issues  caused  by  shutter  glasses,  notably  significant fatigue for the audience. Practically, a shutter mode LED 3D system is simply a standard 2D screen with a frame frequency doubler. The main problems in a shutter-mode LED 3D system are:

- 3.1 This explains how, in a shutter mode system, one eye can see while the other cannot, and vice versa. The principle of double-image 3D relies on our brain's central processor, which must receive both images simultaneously to analyze and process them rapidly. This allows us to experience three-dimensional sensations through what could be called our 'third eye.' However, since we can only see one image at a time, it raises questions of how the brain performs these calculations.  This necessitates some form of temporary memory storage for the images. The brain's reflexive cells play a crucial role in handling this task. In shutter-mode systems, many neural cells involved in short-term memory must work intensively to store alternating images. This is why in a shutter mode system, the 'fatigue' produced. In contrast, in polarizing-mode systems, the brain does not need to perform this additional memory-intensive process.

Fig. 3.1 A tomato is thrown out from a 3D screen, almost touching the audience's face, with the ROCOS reaching over 95%.


- 3.2 Fast 2D or 3D movement of objects within a 3D video can cause distortion or a reduction in 3D resolution.
- 3.3 In a modern LED display, the scanning process differs significantly from that of a projector. In a shutter mode system, the input video displays operate at 60Hz. After frame frequency doubling, the frame rate changes, as illustrated in Fig. 3.2. Originally, the display period is 1/60 = 16.7 ms. After doubling the frame frequency, this period is reduced to 8.3 ms. The refresh rate of an LED screen can be as high as 1200 Hz, which means one period is now only 0.83ms. For high-quality shutter glasses, the switching time is approximately 2 ms. Consequently, some parts of the picture may be cut off. However, this loss does not occur in a polarizing system.

Fig. 3.2 Schematic of some picture fields lost in a shutter mode 3D.


## 4. CONCLUSION

In  conclusion,  the  "LED  3D  Cinema  Display"  system  not  only  eliminates  the  risk  of  '3D  vertigo syndrome,'  a  common  issue  with  projector  systems,  but  also  exhibits  significantly  less  crosstalk compared to projectors. Additionally, several other advantages are worth considering. For instance, there is no need for 'dark adaptation' when entering the theater or 'bright adaptation' upon leaving,

which is beneficial for protecting visual health. This is why the 3D LED Cinema Display system will inevitably replace 3D projection.

Even with the polarized 3D LED movie player, "3D vertigo syndrome" will not occur naturally; however, it can be artificially produced. This is very useful for further study of "3D vertigo."

What was the initial impact of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) on free-viewpoint rendering, and how have subsequent advancements, such as 3D Gaussian Splatting, addressed its early limitations to optimize rendering workflows and achieve higher visual quality for digital assets?

<1-hop>

# 

# Advancements in Radiance Field Techniques for Volumetric Video Generation: A Technical Overview

Joshua Maraval 1,2 , Nicolas Ramin 1 and Lu Zhang 1,2

1 IRT b<>com, France and 2 CNRS, IETR-UMR 6164, France
Joshua.maraval@insa-rennes.fr

ABSTRACT

Video consumption has grown rapidly worldwide, supported by advanced devices such as smartphones, tablets, and immersive headsets like Apple Vision Pro, which enable real-time 6 Degrees of Freedom (6DoF) navigation. Yet, the lack of engaging volumetric content limits applications in training and entertainment.

Volumetric video offers promise but faces challenges in natural 3D+t reconstruction, coding, and rendering due to high computational demands. In 2020, the ground-breaking Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) paper introduced a new way to generate natural free-viewpoint renderings of real scenes.

Follow-up research, including 3D Gaussian Splatting, improved efficiency and flexibility, though most approaches still require separate models per frame, complicating video representation. Recent extensions leverage temporal redundancy for compact, consistent, and editable volumetric video.

This paper reviews state-of-the-art radiance field–based methods, analysing their strengths and limitations, and provides an objective evaluation using a diverse multi-view dataset, with a focus on applications for entertainment and training.

**Keywords:** volumetric video, neural radiance fields, 3D Gaussian Splatting, free-viewpoint rendering, immersive media

Introduction

Novel view synthesis (NVS) is a long-standing challenge of 3D computer vision: the rendering of unseen views of a scene from a set of captured views. NVS has a growing impact on a wide array of video applications including media consumption [1], sports retransmission [2], immersive training [3] and telepresence [4]. The applications fall into one of two categories: visual effects or immersive experiences. One common visual effect with NVS is the virtual rendering of non-captured camera movement. An illustrative example is the Intel True View technology [5], which proposes frozen time 360 degree replays of sports stadiums. In contrast, immersive experiences rely on real-time NVS to display position-dependent views to a user, allowing them to navigate freely within a virtual scene as if they were in the real location.

Early NVS methods interpolated viewpoints from depth information [6]. These methods were capable of rendering realistic novel views in ideal conditions, but they had limited light effect rendering capacity and were restricted to rendering views that were close to the reference views. Concurrently, novel devices, including the Apple Vision Pro, were making real-time 6 Degrees of Freedom (6DoF) tracking increasingly accessible. Free navigation of real scenes requires reconstructing a complete representation of the scene from recorded videos. In recent years, significant progress has been made towards volumetric-based approaches. One such approach is Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [7] which was first published in 2020. This method enables the generation of high-quality views by modelling the scene’s geometry and radiance. NeRF demonstrated the capacity of radiance field methods to represent complex real scenes with accurate light effects. Following the publication of NeRF, radiance fields have rapidly become the most regarded approach for NVS of natural content.

Early radiance field methods, including NeRF necessitated slow reconstructions for every scene to be performed, and could not render novel views in real time. New approaches have been derived from NeRF for faster processing [8], [9], higher quality rendering [10], [11] and more stable reconstructions [12]. The recent radiance field method 3D Gaussian Splatting techniques [13] have gained considerable popularity due to their demonstration of state-of-the-art rendering quality with in-real-time rendering capacity.

Building upon the latest advances in radiance field methods, the volumetric video field has undergone a rapid evolution in recent years. New techniques have extended the applicability of radiance field to a range of classical 2D video tasks, including semantic segmentation [14], streaming [15] and edition [16]. The development of real-time dynamic representations of radiance fields has opened the door to 6DoF+t navigable content in real-time.

However, each approach has its own advantages and drawbacks. We present an overview of NVS methods, focusing on radiance field approaches. We review the latest advances towards real-time 6DoF+t navigation and evaluate the state-of-the-art methods on a dataset of scenes showcasing complex human interactions in diverse environments.

NOVEL VIEW SYNTHESIS METHODS


Figure 1 - The input images for NVS undergo a pre-processing calibration step. The camera parameters are retrieved from the input images with the Structure-from-motion software COLMAP. A multi-view Dataset is constituted of the input images and meta parameters of the scene, including camera parameters. We can see above the camera positions and orientations extracted in red after the COLMAP calibration.

From multiple images capturing a single scene, NVS algorithms render novel viewpoints that have not been previously observed. To interpret the image's information, it is necessary to understand the position and orientation of the camera relative to the other images. There exist methods that generate novel views only from input images without requiring prior knowledge of camera parameters, simultaneously based on SLAM [17], [18] or state-of-the-art radiance fields [19], [20], [21]. These camera-parameters free methods are considered out of the scope of this review. This review focuses solely on methods that use known camera parameters of input images. To obtain camera parameters from multi-view images of a scene, a pre-processing step of structure-from-motion is typically used. In this paper, this calibration step is achieved using the structure-from-motion software COLMAP [18], as illustrated in Figure 1.

## Interpolation-based View Synthesis

Interpolation-based NVS methods [Fig. 2] generate novel views by interpolating pixel information between input views . Some approaches, called Depth Image Based Rendering (DIBR) leverage information from the associated depth maps of the input images for more accurate translation of the input pixels to the novel view [6], [22]. DIBR can achieve high-quality rendering of intermediate views but often results in errors at object edges and occluded areas and lacks light effect rendering. Light field approaches [23], [24] interpolate all pixels in an intermediate 3D space, which is then inferred to render novel views. Light fields can render views with complex occlusions and light effects, but this necessitates a dense array of input views.

Figure 2 - Interpolation-based view synthesis. The pixels from the input views are interpolated to render the novel view.

Following the wide introduction of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) based deep learning by Krizhevsky et al. in 2012 [25], CNNs gained popularity for view synthesis methods. In recent works, CNNs have been trained as a post-filter to improve the rendered images of DIBR-based methods, effectively removing some artifacts [26]. Other methods train a CNN-based architecture in place of the interpolation function for DIBR [27]. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated that a few images of a scene can be used to predict other views [28], [29] or enhance NVS renders [11]. While methods based on deep CNNs for NVS may generate high-quality renders, they are inherently slow to infer which results in low rendering frame rates.

**Learning-based volumetric representations**

The rendering of views from a volumetric representation is a well-studied subject of computer vision. For instance, photorealistic models can be rendered from synthetic scenes modelled as meshes using the latest rendering technologies. However, models used to design synthetic data are limited representations of the real world and differ significantly from the light physics behind human vision. Some works have proposed the use of CNN architectures for higher quality mesh rendering [30], [31], [32]. However, these representations are partially differentiable, which makes them difficult to optimize without a high density of input images. Seminal works proposed the use of a plenoptic function as a volumetric representation of scene, capable of rendering light coherent novel views [23], [24]. The plenoptic function is a 5D function describing the light flow at any 3D position of any 2D orientation, as illustrated in Figure 4. Beyond novel view synthesis, this representation is also useful for 3D rendering on automultiscopic and light field displays, as well as diffractive holographic displays, where capturing and reproducing the full flow of light is essential. With recent advances in machine learning, a learning-based approach has become a viable option for novel view synthesis.


Figure 3 - 3D Model learning-based View synthesis from volumetric representation. A volumetric representation of the scene is reconstructed from the input images. After complete training, novel views are rendered by inference of the volumetric representation.

Most modern approaches to learning-based volumetric representations feature a complete or partial representation of the plenoptic function. A generic workflow is presented in Figure 3. Prior to rendering novel views, the volumetric representation must be reconstructed from the input images. Input views are rendered from the representation, and then an error loss is computed based on the difference between the rendered image and the reference images. The loss is then propagated backwards to adjust the volumetric model parameters into a new model that more closely renders the reference images, until complete convergence is achieved.

Multi-plane images (MPI) approaches divide the plenoptic function into successive planes that store color and transparency information [33], [34], [35]. While these approaches are fast and capable of photorealistic renderings, MPI are limited to rendering views facing a single direction, as a perpendicular view to the planes cannot be rendered. Broxton et al. [36] demonstrated that a structure of spherical planes can be used for efficient 360° scene rendering, with the limitation that rendered views must be close to the circle's center. $\varphi$

Figure 4 - Plenoptic function illustration. For a given position (x,y,z), a viewing direction ( $\varphi , \theta$ ), the plenoptic function returns the intensity of light observed across time at any frequency observed.

**Neural radiance fields**

**NeRF**


The Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) model, published in 2021 by Mildenhall et al. [7], marked a significant shift in the field of volumetric rendering. The paper attracted considerable and growing attention, as evidenced by the citations graph in Figure 5. NeRF  introduces a fully connected deep network that outputs volume density and view-dependent radiance at any point in space. A ray-casting strategy is proposed to retrieve the colors of any view. The pixel ray is projected into the three-dimensional space, sampled into three-dimensional points, and the density and radiance of each point are inferred by a multilayer perceptron (MLP). The pixel color is obtained with a classical ray-casting rendering. The MLP is trained from scratch for any new scene reconstruction. NeRF is a powerful representation capable of generating photorealistic renders of complex scenes and a flexible and simple volumetric representation.

Following the introduction of NeRF, numerous radiance field architectures have been proposed. IBRNet [37] blends classical interpolation-based view synthesis with a non-scene-specific radiance field MLP. Optimized radiance field architectures have been demonstrated to have real-time rendering capacities [38], [39], [40]. More efficient sampling strategies have been studied for faster rendering [41], with anti-aliased and generalizable NeRF for boundless scenes [10], [42]. Many extensions of radiance fields have been proposed to extend the applications to other research fields. Large-scale NeRF extend the capacities of radiance fields to city-scale models [43], [44], [45]. Other contributions on scene understanding integrate NeRF into a scene graph [46], [47], for an editable volumetric representation. A large amount of NeRF studies are focused on more specific tasks such as avatar or face reconstruction [48], [49], [50].


Figure 6 - Radiance Fields reconstruction pipeline.

Reconstruction of radiance fields from a limited set of views is possible, but failure may occur if the captured views are too sparse [Fig. 6]. The reconstruction process involves recovering a 5D function from 2D images, which is an under-resolved problem. Significant advances have been made in improving radiance field stability with regularizations, which are rules to constrain the radiance field function to converge towards a coherent model. Three main regularizations have greatly improved radiance field stability. The homogeneity regularization, proposed as Total Variation (TV) by Lombardi et al. [51], encourages the model to have homogeneous zones. This means that the model must feature compact objects with diffuse color. The regularization can be applied on 3D points [8], [52], [53] or encouraged on adjacent pixels of the rendered views [12], [54], [55]. Sparsity regularization encourages the emptiness of the model, thereby reducing the occurrence of unstructured artifacts. Beta-loss [8], [51], [51], Cauchy-loss [8], [39], [56] and entropy loss [53], [54] have been demonstrated to be efficient losses for sparsity regularization. Finally, appearance regularization encourages renders to appear correct, with the use of a trained CNN [12] or GAN architecture to guide and refine rendered patches [11].

Table 1 - Overview of regularization methods proposed in state-of-the-art Radiance Field papers for reconstruction stability. We classify approaches into three categories: scene homogeneity, sparsity and appearance regularization. Either samples/3D points or rays associated with pixels can be regularized.

**Spatially Encoded Radiance Fields**

NeRF represents a significant advance in the field of computer vision, but it comes at a cost. The MLP, a key component of the NeRF model, is a relatively slow network to infer, requiring multiple inferences for a single pixel. One of the major advances in radiance field research has been the simplification of the implicit radiance function. To reduce the complexity load on the MLP, it can be spatially decomposed into smaller functions, as demonstrated in [57]. Yu et al. demonstrated that the radiance function can be reduced to a simple MLP-free representation, encoding density directly and orientation-dependent color in a simple parametrization [8], [56].

Other research has investigated the use of a voxel grid to store feature vectors in the three-dimensional space. The feature vectors are trained alongside the MLP [53] and inputted to the MLP depending on the sampling location. The volumetric model information is divided into smaller batches that are more focused on local features. Consequently, rendering quality equal to or higher than NeRF can be achieved with a smaller MLP architecture, resulting in faster rendering. As demonstrated in [39] and [58], feature vectors can be stored in sparse voxel grids. Müller et al. developed Instant-NeRF [59] a multi-resolution feature voxel grid-based radiance field, which enables the rendering of higher-quality radiance with faster rendering speeds, see Figure 7.


Figure 7 - Example representation of spatially encoded radiance field.





3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a method published in 2023 [13] that has rapidly gained recognition in volumetric reconstruction research. It is commonly associated with radiance field methods and is a differentiable point cloud-based approach for learning-based volumetric rendering. The 3DGS model is composed of 3D Gaussians with geometry, orientation–dependent color and density trainable parameters. Novel views are rendered through rasterization of the Gaussians onto the new view image plane, which is a faster process than ray casting, while maintaining most properties of radiance field rendering. In contrast to previous learning-based point cloud rendering approaches [32], 3DGS generates and prunes points during reconstruction, and is not dependent on a dense point cloud initialization.

Figure 8 - Illustration of the temporal flickering in Gaussian Splatting renderings of adjacent frames on the Carpark scene [60]

Radiance field methods are flexible yet powerful trainable representations of 3D scenes. Intuitively, training radiance field models using successive video frames as input results in a 4D representation of a dynamic scene. While this is true, the lack of temporal constraints associated with the underlying under-resolution of the radiance field reconstruction results in temporal artefacts during rendering of dynamic scenes. Figure 8 illustrates the flickering that can occur with sparse input views. The phenomenon of flickering is particularly evident in reconstructed zones with a higher degree of shape ambiguity, where numerous potential reconstructions could satisfy the reference images rendering. Consequently, windows reflections and occluded areas exhibit more pronounced flickering artefacts.

**Dynamic Radiance Fields**

The integration of the temporal dimension in a radiance field-based volumetric representation offers two benefits. Firstly, it increases temporal homogeneity, reinforcing spatial information with temporal redundancy. Secondly, it addresses temporary occluded areas. Deformation-based approaches achieve this by dividing the dynamic radiance field into a spatial radiance field and a dynamic deformation field [49], [61], [62]. All temporal instants respect morphologically consistent changes. Similar proposals have been published for dynamic 3DGS [63], [64]. Other dynamic radiance field papers demonstrate excellent performance by inputting the temporal dimension to a first MLP [15] or the feature grid [65].

In contrast to NeRF-based methods, 3DGS features a fully explicit volumetric model that can be more directly extended to the temporal dimension. Yang et al. [66] extend the 3D Gaussians with a temporal dimension and constrain them to coherent movement. In SpaceTime Gaussian Feature Splatting (STG) [67], polynomials are trained to represent the 3D Gaussians movement, forcing smooth movement.

METHODs COMPARISON

The comparison of Radiance Field methods is a challenging task, given it is an evolving field. Evaluation of methods is often conducted on older datasets that may not fully reflect the capabilities of state-of-the-art methods. Many methods have metadata prerequisites, such as the scene bounding box or depth maps. Moreover, a significant number of radiance field implementations are designed for specific content, such as full-frontal views, inside captures and concentric views. We evaluate the methods on scenes of the MUVOD Dataset [68], a compilation of multi-view video sequences from various sources. The sequences feature varied content, environments, and capture rigs, and include scenes focusing on human interaction.

The evaluation dataset comprises 14 sequences made of between 8 and 30 views. The view calibration is conducted using COLMAP [18]. One middle view is excluded from the training and retained for evaluation purposes for each sequence. Following training, the evaluation view is rendered and compared with the reference. The evaluation metrics employed are PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS. PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio) measures how close the pixels of the rendered image are to the reference. SSIM (Structural Similarity Index) measures how well the overall structure and details of the image match the reference. LPIPS (Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity) measures how similar two images appear using features learned from neural networks to approach human subjective judgement. For SSIM and PSNR, higher values are better, while for LPIPS, lower values are better. The rendering time is the average rendering time for a frame. Memory usage is the average size of the volumetric model for a sequence.

The following methods were evaluated: Plenoxels [8], Nerfacto [9], 3DGS [13] and STG [67]. Plenoxels and Nerfacto were selected to represent spatially encoded radiance fields. Nerfacto is a community-driven implementation of Instant-NeRF [59]. Plenoxels is trained on a high-resolution grid of 1024 3 voxels. Both Nerfacto and Plenoxels utilize the COLMAP calibration sparse point cloud, as described in [69], to initialize their bounding boxes. 3DGS is trained for 7000 iterations. The STG method is the only dynamic method of the tested methods and is a dynamic extension of 3DGS. It is evaluated on five frames, and the results are averaged to be equivalent to a single frame, as with the other methods. Other state-of-the-art methods such as Mip-NeRF [10] or GANeRF [11] are not evaluated despite their high rendering quality due to their lengthy training times. The methods are trained with default parameters on a Nvidia A100 GPU, and the results are shown in Table 2.

| Method    | PSNR ↑     | SSIM ↑    | LPIPS ↓   | Recon time ↓   | Memory Usage ↓   |
|-----------|------------|-----------|-----------|----------------|------------------|
| Plenoxels | 22.963     | 0.810     | 0.368     | 45 min         | 2,85 GB          |
| Nerfacto  | 24.662     | 0.816     | 0,261     | **8 min**      | 167 MB           |
| 3DGS      | 27.803     | 0.866     | 0.220     | **8 min**      | 140 MB           |
| STG       | **29.523** | **0.916** | **0.177** | 10 min         | **5 MB**         |

Table 2 - Methods comparison results. Average reconstruction and rendering metrics over 14 multi-view sequences.

Compared to all three other methods, Plenoxels has lower performance for each metric. Plenoxels' regular voxel grid stores feature vectors at the same resolution throughout the scene. This results in suboptimal information resolution for reconstructing foreground content, which has a higher resolution in reference images. In Figure 9, the foreground content is visibly blurred for the Plenoxels renders. This data structure also results in long training times and higher memory consumption compared to other methods.

Nerfacto performs significantly worse than 3DGS and STG on all rendering quality metrics but has the lowest reconstruction time, tied with 3DGS and a comparable memory usage to 3DGS. Renders of two scenes are shown in Figure 9. The rendering quality of Nerfacto is very high for simple content like the car, but the reconstruction is particularly unstable for more complex scenes. For example, the people in the background in the lower image are poorly reconstructed due to occlusions from the people in the foreground.

3DGS and STG have the best rendering quality compared to the other two methods. The 3D Gaussians are a powerful and flexible representation. Even for difficult scenes, the training converges to a coherent geometry due to the point cloud initialization with COLMAP. 3DGS and related work are a promising solution for reliable high quality volumetric video with real-time rendering.



Figure 9 – Renders from sequences PoznanStreet [60] and MartialArts [70]

STG renders have better quality for every metric compared to all three other methods. This demonstrates the benefit of temporal information that can resolve occlusion ambiguities. If part of the scene is visible in the other training frames, this information constrains the occluded area to coherent content. The average reconstruction time of STG for a single frame is comparable to 3DGS and Nerfacto and could be reduced by training with more frames. STG has significantly lower memory consumption than the other methods evaluated. A single model is used for all five frames, resulting in an optimized, memory efficient model that could be further optimized by training on a larger number of frames.

The image metrics used evaluate images independently, and the video rendering of STG is not compared to the reference video. However, there is a strong gain in temporal stability of the renders compared to training independent frames with 3DGS. Figure 8 illustrates the rendering of independent frames and Figure 10 illustrates the simultaneous training of multiple frames with STG. Temporal flickering is visible for 3DGS in areas of ambiguous geometry, while renders are coherent for STGFS in static areas. While this can have an important impact on subjective quality, it is a missing piece of information for PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, which are the metrics classically used for volumetric video quality evaluation.





Figure 10 - Illustration of the temporal stability in Spacetime Gaussian Feature Splatting renderings of adjacent frames models on the Carpark scene [60]

CONCLUSIONS

In this paper, we provided an overview of volumetric video, focusing on recent advances in radiance fields for real-time free navigation of natural content. Advances in radiance field training and rendering optimization, reconstruction stability, and temporal expansion were detailed. The performance of state-of-the-art radiance field methods was evaluated in terms of objective metrics, training complexity, and memory usage on a multi-view video dataset of complex scenes.

Since the introduction of NeRF in 2021, volumetric video has steadily evolved towards reliable application in real-world use cases. Radiance Field methods continue to improve and are close to being mature enough for widespread use. Volumetric video could be the long-awaited answer to the lack of engaging content on immersive displays, helping content providers create immersive experiences with minimal production costs.

reference: The Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) model, introduced in 2020, marked a significant shift in volumetric rendering by providing a ground-breaking way to generate natural free-viewpoint renderings of real scenes. NeRF enabled the generation of high-quality views by modeling a scene's geometry and radiance, demonstrating the capacity to represent complex real scenes with accurate light effects and quickly becoming a highly regarded approach for novel view synthesis. However, early NeRF methods necessitated slow reconstructions for every scene and could not render novel views in real time. Subsequent advancements have addressed these limitations to optimize rendering workflows and achieve higher visual quality. For instance, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), published in 2023, has gained considerable popularity due to its demonstration of state-of-the-art rendering quality with in-real-time rendering capacity. 3DGS renders novel views through rasterization of 3D Gaussians onto the image plane, a process faster than NeRF's ray casting, while maintaining most properties of radiance field rendering. In comparative evaluations, 3DGS achieved superior rendering quality metrics (PSNR 27.803, SSIM 0.866, LPIPS 0.220) with a reconstruction time of 8 minutes and memory usage of 140 MB, outperforming methods like Plenoxels and Nerfacto in quality and matching Nerfacto's speed. This makes 3DGS a promising solution for reliable high-quality volumetric video with real-time rendering, directly contributing to optimized rendering workflows and precise visual fidelity for digital assets.

## Scalable AI-Powered Content-Adaptive Encoding for NextGen Video Delivery

Savi Shi

VisualOn, Inc.

## Written for presentation at the

## SMPTE 2025 Media and Technology Summit

Abstract. Content-Adaptive Encoding (CAE) has emerged as a practical method for reducing bitrate while preserving or improving visual quality. This paper introduces a machine learning-based CAE approach developed by VisualOn, which employs single-pass prediction and real-time adaptation to dynamically optimize encoding parameters. Benchmark results across AVC, HEVC, AV1, and multiple hardware platforms demonstrate average bitrate reductions between 20% and 50%, with consistent quality improvements measured by VMAF. Case studies confirm bitrate savings in production environments, alongside reduced startup delay and buffering. Tests on Intel Xeon processors, Intel Data Center GPU Flex Series, NVIDIA NVENC, Qualcomm ARM devices, and ASIC encoders suggest that the approach is broadly applicable across diverse platforms.

Keywords. Content-adaptive encoding, machine learning, video compression, VMAF, FFmpeg, Intel Xeon, live streaming, VoD

## Introduction

Video consumption continues to grow rapidly, placing pressure on delivery and storage infrastructures. Traditional static encoding ladders are inefficient because they do not adapt to scene complexity, motion, or texture. This leads to higher than necessary bitrates and increased costs.

In 2015, Netflix introduced per-title encoding, followed by per-chunk encoding in 2016 and pershot encoding in 2018, which demonstrated average bitrate reductions of more than 30% without perceptible quality loss [1][2]. Building on this evolution, machine learning-based CAE applies dynamic optimization at the frame and segment level, adjusting encoder parameters in real time. Unlike codec transitions, this approach can be integrated into existing workflows with minimal disruption.

## Business Case and Benefits of CAE

The rapid growth of video consumption places increasing pressure on delivery and storage infrastructure. For a streaming service with 1 million subscribers, each watching an average of 1 hour per day at a 3 Mbps bitrate, the annual content delivery network (CDN) cost at $0.001 per GB would amount to approximately $492,275. Similarly, maintaining 5 PB of archived content would cost $250,000 for local storage at $50 per TB, or around $300,000 annually for cloud storage at $5 per TB per month. Reducing bitrates without sacrificing visual quality is therefore critical for controlling operational expenses.

Prior evaluations [3] have consistently shown that per-title and content-adaptive encoding (CAE) methods improve streaming efficiency by dynamically adjusting encoding parameters to the characteristics of each video. These studies demonstrate that CAE optimizes bitrate allocation at the title, segment, or scene level, taking into account motion, texture, and scene complexity. This adaptive approach not only reduces overall bitrate but also supports a wide range of devices and network conditions, simplifies management of large video libraries, and improves delivery flexibility.

Building on this foundation, the VisualOn Optimizer has demonstrated bitrate savings ranging from 20% to 50% [4], depending on codec and platform. Beyond cost reduction, CAE enhances quality consistency by allocating bits according to scene complexity, resulting in fewer visible artifacts in high-motion segments and more efficient compression in simpler scenes. Users benefit from shorter startup times and fewer rebuffering events. From an operational perspective, CAE reduces storage requirements for mezzanine and archival assets, scales effectively for 4K, 8K, and emerging formats, and can be integrated into existing device ecosystems without requiring client-side changes.

## Workflow of the Optimizer

The workflow begins with feature extraction, where spatial and temporal characteristics of video frames are analyzed. A one-pass machine learning framework predicts encoding parameters such as bitrate, GOP (Group of Pictures) size, and rate control for each segment. Training is performed using particle swarm optimization, and the trained model is applied in production through lightweight classifiers. A feedback mechanism evaluates output quality using metrics including VMAF, PSNR, and SSIM, and adjusts parameters dynamically.

Different implementations are suited to specific use cases. Optimizer Live supports real-time streaming with no additional latency. Optimizer VOD enables efficient per-segment adaptation across entire ABR ladders. Optimizer Fidelity targets visually lossless compression of mezzanine content [4].

Figure1. VisualOn Optimizer integrates into any streaming workflow.

<!-- image -->

## Test Bed and Performance Evaluation

Testing was conducted using the framework from Ozer [1] on 21 clips representing diverse categories. On an Intel i7-13700H with VMAF target set to 96, comparisons with FFmpeg encoders showed consistent improvements. For H.264, average bitrate was reduced by 42% with an 8.4-point VMAF gain and 15% CPU savings. For HEVC, reductions averaged 38% with quality improvements around 9 VMAF points. For AV1, average savings were 17% with similar quality gains and modest additional CPU usage.

To provide a fuller picture, future work will report averages, variance, and worst-case scenarios alongside peak savings, as 'up to' values may overstate real-world impact.

## Intel Xeon, GPU, and Mobile Results

Extended tests confirmed scalability across hardware platforms. On Intel Xeon Scalable processors with Quick Sync Video, bitrate reductions were 44% for H.264, 39% for HEVC, and 16% for AV1, with consistent quality improvements. NVIDIA NVENC showed 18-20% reductions with quality gains of 6-9 VMAF points. Qualcomm ARM-based mobile testing showed over 23% bitrate savings. ASIC encoders achieved 35-46% savings with about 2-point VMAF improvements [4][6].

## Real-World Production Results

Deployment results support the benchmark findings. At Intigral, the average bitrate dropped from 3.0 Mbps to 1.36 Mbps (-54.7%), startup delay was reduced by 18%, and buffering ratio improved by 5% [5]. Table 1 below shows the comparison of Intigral's operation results before and after adopting Optimizer. EiTV in Brazil integrated the system within one week and achieved over 40% average bitrate reduction [6]. These cases highlight potential, though broader datasets and multi-operator validation would provide stronger generalizability.

Table 1. x264 vs. Optimizer with x264

## Comparative Context

While our benchmark results focus on FFmpeg x264/x265, it is worth noting that other CAE approaches take different adaptation strategies. For example, Netflix applies per-shot encoding with perceptual optimization, and Harmonic's EyeQ employs AI-enhanced content-aware techniques. In contrast, the VisualOn Optimizer performs dynamic adaptation at both frame and

segment levels within a unified machine learning framework, reducing reliance on manual heuristics or shot segmentation.

## Advancements and Integration

The approach has been fully integrated into FFmpeg for AVC, HEVC, and AV1. It has also been demonstrated for real-time streaming, including proof-of-concept implementations on Snapdragon-based mobile devices. Its machine learning framework is covered by granted and pending patents, and is already in production with multiple operators [4].

## Limitations and Future Work

While CAE shows significant promise, several limitations remain. Training models requires curated datasets and computational resources, and generalization across highly diverse content types may require ongoing retraining. Objective metrics including VMAF, PSNR, and SSIM were used to quantify quality improvements in a reproducible manner across multiple codecs and platforms. While these metrics do not fully capture perceptual experience, structured subjective testing is planned to complement the current evaluation and validate perceived visual quality under diverse viewing conditions. For live streaming, very low-latency scenarios and rapid scene changes, such as in sports, remain challenging. Future work will focus on expanding subjective validation, refining models for real-time adaptation, and extending CAE to new formats such as HDR, 8K, and immersive media.

## Conclusion

Content-Adaptive Encoding provides an effective means of reducing video delivery costs and improving quality without requiring changes in client devices. The Optimizer framework achieves consistent bitrate savings of 20-50%, quality gains measured by VMAF, and scalability across CPU, GPU, ARM, and ASIC platforms. Production results show encouraging benefits, though broader validation-including subjective testing and comparisons with alternative CAE methods-is needed. Continued research on live-readiness and real-time adaptation will help CAE evolve into a robust, widely adopted approach for next-generation video delivery.

Abstract. Technical Recommendations TR-07 and TR-08 were originally developed by the Video Services Forum (VSF) to provide an interoperable method for the transport of low latency JPEG XS coded video over LAN and WAN IP networks.

## Introduction

The Video Services Forum (VSF) is actively revising TR-07 and TR-08 to mainly focus on improving clarity, consistency, and real-world interoperability. This latest revision also incorporates JPEG XS Temporal Differential Coding (TDC), a new predictive wavelet-based compression method that uses previously compressed frames to boost coding efficiency

The revised recommendations define:

- Broader Enhancements to TR-07 and TR-08 documents to improve interoperability and interlace handling, including refined buffer models, rate shaping, additional guidance, clarification and constraints along with references to updated industry standards
- Clear interoperability points for JPEG XS TDC and also 444.12 High Profile (which is now expanded to support additional frame rates common in cinema and streaming).
- New Capability Sets for low bandwidth use cases

The objectives of this paper/presentation are to:

- 1) Provide broader insight and appreciation of the updates to the TR-07 and TR-08 recommendations in support of enhanced interoperability and future-ready media workflows.
- 2) Present the integration of JPEG-XS Temporal Differential Coding (TDC) into TR-07 and TR-08 and highlight its salient characteristics. (It is NOT the intention of this paper/presentation to get into an in-depth TDC description and/or comparative analysis. Only a simplified overview and block diagram are provided.)
- 3) Propose expanded capability sets and interoperability points

## Video Services Forum (VSF) Technical Recommendations - TR-07 & TR-08

The Video Services Forum (VSF) is an industry association founded in the late 1990's to promote interoperability and innovation in video networking technologies. It brings together broadcasters, manufacturers, and service providers to develop open standards and best practices for professional media transport-especially over IP. VSF helped define standards like SMPTE ST 2022 and ST 2110, and protocols like RIST (Reliable Internet Stream Transport).

Its pivotal technical recommendations TR-07 and TR-08 , have shaped modern IP video transport.

- TR-07 defines how to transport JPEG XS compressed video using MPEG-2 Transport Streams (TS) over IP networks and is ideal for legacy broadcast workflows.  It was first published in 2021 with the latest revision in April 2022, and enables low-latency, high-quality video transport with JPEG XS compression.
- TR-08 outlines the transport of JPEG XS video within the ST 2110-22 framework, which is part of the broader SMPTE ST 2110 suite for professional media over IP. It too was first published in 2021 with the latest revision also dated in 2022. TR-08 was designed for modern/current IP-based production environments, enabling broadcast quality, virtually lossless compressed video transport with ultra-low latency

## Interoperability Testing & Evolution

In 2022, VSF conducted a file exchange program for TR-07 and TR-08, allowing vendors to test RTP (Real-Time Transport Protocol) file compatibility. This led to:

- Ø Identification of anomalies and ambiguities
- Ø Clarifications in the TR documents
- Ø Improved interoperability across implementations

These TRs are foundational for integrating JPEG XS into both legacy and next-gen workflows, and can be found on the VSF Technical Recommendations page.

## Currently Supported Frame Rates in TR-07 and TR-08

In terms of broadcast frame rates, both TR-07 (JPEG XS over MPEG-2 TS) and TR-08 (JPEG XS over SMPTE ST 2110-22) are designed to be flexible and interoperable across common industry formats. Below is a summary of the typical frame rates supported:

| Format Resolution   | Common Frame Rates Supported   |
|---------------------|--------------------------------|
| 720p                | 50, 59.94, fps                 |
| 1080i               | 25, 29.97, fps (interlaced)    |
| 1080p               | 50, 59.94, fps                 |
| 4K UHD              | 50, 59.94, fps                 |
| 8K UHD              | 50, 59.94, fps (optional)      |

These frame rates align with standard broadcast formats and are validated through interoperability points defined in the TR documents. The VSF also conducted file exchange testing with 1080p and 1080i JPEG XS streams to ensure compatibility across vendors.

In working with specialized formats (e.g., RGB 4:4:4, 12-bit, or multimedia extensions), TR08 especially provides flexibility for those use cases as well.

## TR-07/TR-08 Revision Activity Group

The VSF TR-07/TR-08 JPEG XS TDC Revision Activity Group is a focused industry effort to update the Video Services Forum's TR-07 and TR-08 technical recommendations. Thirty-four (34) VSF members, composed of end-users, service providers & manufacturers, are part of this effort.

This group was formed to:

- Clarify ambiguities in the current documents for seamless interoperability between different vendors
- Integrate the latest/newest edition of JPEG XS, JPEG XS TDC (Temporal Differential Coding) into TR-07 (MPEG-2 TS transport) and TR-08 (SMPTE ST 211022 transport)
- Define capability sets for TDC

## Key Technical Objectives as determined by the VSF Revision Activity Group

- Ø Improve interoperability by refining header definitions, timestamping, and interlace handling
- Ø Add TDC capability sets , covering:
- o Sync/Async modes
- o IPMX compatibility
- o Resolutions: FHD, 4K, 8K

## Goals of this Activity Group Effort

- a)  Address and add JPEG XS Temporal Differential Coding
- b) Collaborate with IETF on revision to RFC9134
- c) Add new TDC capability sets and interop points
- d) Add new interop points for non-broadcast frame rates -23.98, 24, 29.97, 30 & 60 fps
- e) Add specific capability set for 1Gb max trunks
- f) Update Normative Reference Section to include current documents
- g) Add Traffic Shaping and Delivery Timing
- h) Provide clarifications for better understanding and consistent implementations

Figure 1 - Goals of the Activity Group Effort

- a): Address & Add JPEG XS Temporal Differential Coding (reference Figure 1)

JPEG XS Temporal Differential Coding (TDC) is a powerful enhancement to the JPEG XS codec, designed for ultra-low latency, visually lossless video compression:

## What Is TDC?

Temporal Differential Coding (TDC) is a relatively new profile introduced in the third edition of JPEG XS. It adds temporal prediction in the wavelet domain , allowing the codec to exploit similarities between consecutive frames without using motion compensation. (Figures 2 and 3)

TDC introduces a new wavelet-based predictive compression tool that enables better coding efficiency by referencing prior frames stored in a compressed memory buffer. This approach can either improve visual quality at a fixed bit rate or enable reduced bandwidth without sacrificing fidelity, all at very low processing latency, which is key for scalable media transport applications in broadcast and professional AV environments.

- The TDC profile makes use of a new coding tool that allows the wavelet coefficients to be predicted from a frame buffer. The frame buffer is a compressed memory buffer that always keeps track of the last version of the wavelet coefficients. So, it is continuously updated with each new frame that is being processed.
- XS TDC comes with a 'frame buffer level' which is essentially a number that can set an upper limit to the size and bandwidth of the frame buffer memory (to control mostly the extra hardware complexity regarding memory).
- Allowed FBB levels are 3 bpp, 4.5 bpp, and 12 bpp (higher FBB level gives better TDC improvements but also leads to bigger needed frame buffer memory).
- TDC can optimize quality at a given rate or allow reduced bit rates for some content

Figure 2 - JPEG XS TDC Highlights

## Key Features

- Ø Single Frame Buffer Prediction : TDC uses a compressed memory buffer to track wavelet coefficients from the previous frame, enabling efficient prediction for semi-static regions.
- Ø No Motion Compensation Needed : Unlike traditional inter-frame codecs, TDC avoids complex algorithms, keeping latency ultra-low and complexity minimal.
- Ø Preserves JPEG XS Strengths :
- o Near-lossless quality
- o Line-based latency (just a few lines delay)
- o Low power and low complexity
- o Hardware-friendly (CPU, GPU, FPGA, ASIC support)

## Performance Gains of TDC versus High profile JPEG XS

- Improved Compression Efficiency : Especially effective for graphics-heavy content like gaming, e-sports, and desktop video.
- PSNR Boosts : Experiments show up to 10 dB improvement in Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio for static or semi-static scenes.

- Graceful Fallback : The TDC profiles also include the High profile, so on high-motion content, a TDC implementation  can be set  to JPEG XS High profile performance, ensuring robustness across various scenarios.

## Compatibility

TDC is designed as an upgrade for existing JPEG XS ecosystems, ensuring seamless integration and future-proofing for broadcast & professional media workflows.

If working in broadcast, live production, or AV-over-IP, TDC balances quality, bandwidth, and latency. Although beyond the scope of this paper, TDC compares quite favorably to other mezzanine level codecs in processing graphics, e-sports, gaming, and complex, low-motion desktop imagery, better preserving details and sharp edges.

Figure 3 - Continued Evolution of JPEG XS


## Courtesy of and with permission from IntoPix

## b): Collaborate with IETF on revision to RFC9134

The Video Services Forum (VSF) TR-07 & TR-08 Revision Activity Group is actively collaborating with the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) on a revision to RFC 9134 , which defines the RTP Payload Format for JPEG XS (ISO/IEC 21122) and is specifically referenced in TR-08.  The amended new RFC will be referenced in the revised version of TR-08.

VSF is also coordinating with IntoPIX and Fraunhofer , key contributors to JPEG XS technology, to ensure the proposed changes are technically sound and widely supported.

## Key Focus of the IETF RFC Revision

- Incorporation of JPEG XS Temporal Differential Coding (TDC):
- o TDC introduces a new coding tool that predicts wavelet coefficients from a compressed frame buffer.
- o This enables better compression efficiency and reduced bitrates while maintaining quality.
- o VSF proposes adding TDC capability sets to the IETF specification, which would obsolete RFC 9134 and lead to a new RFC publication.
- Capability Sets & Interoperability Points:
- o VSF is working on defining new capability sets for TDC across formats like FHD, 4K, 8K, and IPMX.
- o These would be integrated into TR-08 Section 10 and reflected in the updated IETF RFC.

## Encouraging Participation:

- VSF has invited its members to join the IETF process to help shape the new RFC and ensure alignment with industry needs. Currently the revised RFC is in ballot for adoption.

## c): Add new TDC capability sets and interop points

Section 8 of VSF TR-07 focuses on Capability Sets and Interoperability Points for JPEG XS video transported over MPEG-2 Transport Streams using SMPTE ST 2022-2. While the current published version of TR-07 (as of April 2022) does not yet include Temporal Differential Coding (TDC) , updates are underway to incorporate it into future revisions. (Figure 4)

## Section 8 Overview (Current TR-07)

This section defines:

- Capability Sets : Groupings of supported video formats, frame rates, color sampling, and bit depths
- Interoperability Points : Specific combinations that vendors can implement to ensure compatibility across systems

These sets are designed to support:

- HD, 4K, and 8K resolutions
- 4:2:2 and 4:4:4 chroma sampling
- 8-bit and 10-bit depth
- HDR and Wide Color Gamut (WCG)

## Upcoming TDC Enhancements

The VSF JPEG XS Activity Group is working to revise TR-07 to include:

- TDC Capability Sets
- TDC Interop Points

## e): Add specific capability set for 1Gb max trunks

For transport links limited to a 1Gbps max trunk bandwidth, a specific capability set is being defined in the TR-08 revision for both JPEG XS with Temporal Differential Coding (TDC) as well as JPEG XS High Profile. It's aimed at ensuring that JPEG XS TDC and High Profile can both be deployed efficiently in bandwidth-constrained environments like 1 GbE IPMX or ProAV networks, without sacrificing interoperability. Note that this capability set will include the new frame rates as mentioned in Figure 6.

## Capability Set for 1 Gbps Max Trunks (Draft Revision)

Purpose: To define an interoperability point that guarantees a JPEG XS TDC as well as JPEG XS High Profile stream will fit within a 1 Gbps link, including RTP/UDP/IP overhead, for TR-08 (ST 2110-22 over RTP). (Figure 7 )

- Add capability set for maximum Bpp of 2.0, with setting of Sublev 2bpp for:
- Ø TR-08 Capability Set E & ET (TDC) 720p, 1080i FHD
- Ø TR-08 Capability Set E & ET (TDC) 1080p, 2160P UHD1

- Guarantees fit for both JPEG XS TDC and JPEG XS High Profile on 1 GbE links without over-subscription

reference:
The Video Services Forum (VSF) TR-08 outlines the transport of JPEG XS video within the SMPTE ST 2110-22 framework, designed for modern IP-based production environments to enable broadcast quality, virtually lossless compressed video transport with ultra-low latency. The ongoing revisions to TR-08 are actively incorporating Temporal Differential Coding (TDC) into this JPEG XS transport framework over SMPTE ST 2110-22. This integration includes defining new TDC capability sets, which will be added to TR-08 Section 10.

To optimize deployment in bandwidth-constrained scenarios, a specific capability set is being defined in the TR-08 revision for both JPEG XS with TDC and JPEG XS High Profile. This set aims to ensure that a stream will fit within a 1 Gbps link, including RTP/UDP/IP overhead, for TR-08 (ST 2110-22 over RTP). This capability set will include new interoperability points for non-broadcast frame rates and define a maximum Bpp of 2.0, with a Sublev 2bpp setting for resolutions such as 720p, 1080i FHD, 1080p, and 2160P UHD1. The efficiency of TDC allows for maintaining visually lossless quality at lower bitrates, which is crucial for these constrained links, ensuring cross-ecosystem compatibility without custom tuning.
